#6676. The Princess of Wales Swaps Her Classic Waves for a Romantic Boho Hairstyle: How to Recreate It

During her three-day tour of India, the Princess of Wales attended the 2026 Earthshot Prize Ceremony in Mumbai. Prince William founded the initiative in 2020, and it awards environmental solutions with grants to scale and advance their projects.

For the event, Kate wore an oxblood, floor-length Anarkali dress by designer Mahima Mahajan and paired it with extra-fluffy, voluminous bohemian curls pinned in a half-updo.

An elegant, extra-glossy wavy hairstyle has long been a beauty signature for the princess, often teamed with a side part, hats, or a polished ponytail. But for the green carpet in India, the royal opted for a much more dramatic style that matches the glamorous mood of her outfit, with tighter, cascading bohemian curls woven into a beautiful half-updo twist for a romantic finish.

"I would create these curls using a medium-sized tong," recommends Philipp Haug, co-founder of Haug London Haus salon. "Take relatively small sections and use the tongs with a twisting technique, curling one section away from the face and alternating with one section towards the face throughout. Slightly root stretch when you come to the top of the head instead of curling too close to the scalp."

To enhance the fluffiness and volume of the curls, shake them out with your fingers instead of combing them.

Your next special occasion hair inspiration, sorted.

#6674. 24 Veil Alternatives for the Bride Who’d Rather Skip Tradition

Some brides consider the wedding veil sacred, whether it’s an heirloom passed down through generations or a sweeping cathedral-length piece they’ve dreamed of since childhood. Others would rather skip tradition altogether, opting for a statement hair accessory in lieu of lace and tulle. Fortunately, there’s no shortage of veil alternatives—and while they’re a natural fit for courthouse weddings, elopements, and intimate vow exchanges, they can easily hold their own at more formal celebrations, too. Take Princess Eugenie, who ditched the veil entirely for her 2018 nuptials, letting a borrowed emerald tiara steal the show. (If a royal can forgo tradition, so can you!) More recently, Dua Lipa paired a custom Schiaparelli suit with a wide-brimmed Stephen Jones hat for her London civil ceremony.

Bridal designers are also going veil-free: Recent collections from Honor, Floure Studio, Vivienne Westwood, House of Gilles, and Elie Saab feature everything from sculptural hats to bows. When picking out your accessory for the big day, think about balance. An ivory headband adds a modern touch to an otherwise classic ball gown. A lace cloche dials up the drama on a minimalist dress, while a flowing, floral-embroidered scarf brings a romantic feel to a courthouse mini. Wearing a suit? A pillbox hat keeps things incredibly chic, whether you’re getting married at City Hall or eloping somewhere far-flung. Once you’ve settled on a style, be sure to bring it to your hair trial so your stylist knows how to incorporate your accessory seamlessly.

Ahead, discover 24 wedding veil alternatives for every type of bride.

Few accessories are as foolproof as a bridal headband, and with so many iterations on the market, it’s easy to find one that feels right for you. Unadorned padded styles from Loeffler Randall and Maison Ola draw instant attention to a low bun or sleek blowout, while a hand-embroidered option from Lock & Co. Hatters adds some sparkle.

If you’re planning a courthouse wedding or just want an accessory with real presence, a bridal hat is hard to beat. These wide-brimmed silhouettes from Maison Michel, Mains de Vapeur, and Eugenia Kim bring all the drama (and welcome shade at an outdoor ceremony). For something smaller, Gigi Burris’s pillbox has a lovely vintage-inspired aesthetic.

Juliet caps, cloches, and jeweled headpieces are heirlooms in the making; unlike delicate tulle, they’re sturdy enough to be passed down and worn again—plus, they have a built-in old-world feel. Alexandra Grecco and Jennifer Behr keep things soft with lace; De La Vali goes all out with a headscarf that drapes elegantly mid-back; Rabanne channels ’20s glamour with a pearl-and-bead design.

Not ready to surrender the movement of a veil? A cape or scarf offers a similar effect—just in a less conventional way. Rat & Boa’s sheer style shimmers with hand-embellished sequins, and Clio Peppiatt’s mini version adds beaded fringe for extra swing. To keep things understated, drape Markarian’s embroidered scarf or Heirlome’s silk stole over your shoulders.

Bows and bridal have always gone hand in hand, and they make for a playful hair accessory for the consummate romantic. These options from Vivienne Westwood, Completedworks, and Oscar de la Renta fit cascading curls especially well. For a subtle nod to the classic veil, go with Kamperett’s oversized piece, which trails all the way to the floor.

Trade your bouquet for blooms in your hair—or (why not!) go all out and wear both. From flower crowns to smaller clips and pins, there are endless ways to work florals into your hairstyle, especially if you consider yourself a boho bride, and picked the pastoral venue to prove it.

#6669. These Were the Breakout Red Carpet Stars of 2026

Whew—what a year it’s been for red carpets, huh? Between awards season, Fashion Month, and Vogue’s weekly celebrity roundups, there’s been plenty of statement looks to take in throughout 2026. And while there were some notable A-list standouts this year—especially those on our annual Best Dressed list—there were also plenty of emerging names who proved their status as notable rising stars.

Below, Vogue rounded up the 10 breakout stars who had especially splashy, career-making years. And better yet, these buzzy actors and singers all come armed with a unique red carpet style. Whether it’s North of North star Anna Lambe’s championing of Indigenous designers, or actor Diego Calva’s slick array of suits worn on his Club Kid press tour, these Hollywood names are making their mark with distinct fashion choices that make them stand out from the pack. (Sure, they have a team of agents and stylists—but you simply can’t buy taste.)

So, without further ado, meet Vogue’s 10 breakout red carpet stars of 2026.

North of North star Anna Lambe was busy promoting the second season of her hit Netflix series this year—and the Indigenous (Inuk) star brought a unique flavor to the red carpets, working with stylist Nadia Pizzimenti. When she wasn’t busy championing Indigenous designers such as Jamie Okuma or Lesley Hampton, you could find her slipping into sleek Louis Vuitton leather pieces—and sitting front row at the show, of course (like a true fashion It girl).

The Scottish actor gained buzz when he joined the Marvel universe this year, starring in the Disney+ series VisionQuest—but his personal style on the red carpet has been just as action-packed as the show. He and his stylist Fabio Immediato have been showcasing how cool, modern, and totally unfussy modern tailoring can be. Those tinted Prada shades at a VisionQuest screening! A fun little Valentino tie at the BAFTA Scotland Awards! Let’s hear it for a man who has fun with dressing up.

What happens when you star in one of the biggest Hollywood franchises, well, ever? Actor Whitney Peak would know: She brought some seriously epic blockbuster fashions to The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping press tour this year. The star and her stylist Karla Welch have leaned into designs that are theatrical and extravagant—a perfect mood for promoting the film, given the Capitol in The Hunger Games is all about excess. Come for the chic Chanel gowns—stay for the Robert Wun bird dress.

Mexican actor Diego Calva may have gained attention for his role as a social worker in Club Kid, but his red carpet style is less club-rat and much more sleek, sexy and refined. He and stylist Ilaria Urbinati’s go-to formula? Injecting classic-cut suits with more unexpected details. Like his bright red Dzojchen suit and polka-dot tie, or black Loewe tuxedo with a bright-yellow shirt and tie. It’s hard to give a timeless two-piece a more irreverent personality, but Calva has it in spades.

Unless you’ve been living under a rock, you’ve come across a dance banger by Adéla this year. (Finish the lyric: “Every single night, I pray that. . .”) The singer has had a breakout year, thanks to her hits-filled album Prima—so much so that she’s playing Coachella next year. And just as stage-worthy is her pop star approach to fashion. Working with stylist Chris Horan (a master of pop style), she’s cultivated a signature look surrounding tight corsets, mini shorts, and of course, her bright pink hair.

You may know Owen Thiele as a pro podcaster (stream “In Your Dreams”) and actor (watch Adults), but the rising star is bringing some sleek attitude to the red carpet scene. He’s been working with stylist Jared Ellner (his IRL boyfriend, fun fact), and his wardrobe for the spotlight centers around giving menswear classics a more youthful twist. Think: A suit vest worn with no shirt underneath, or a classic collared shirt with more than a few buttons unbuttoned. Fierce is fierce, honey.

It’s certainly Sienna Spiro’s year, thanks to her acclaimed debut album Visitor. The English singer won best new artist at this year’s MTV VMAs—and earned the same award nomination at the 2026 Grammys, no less. If one can describe her sound as raspy and powerful, her red carpet style can be labelled as just as soulful: She works with stylist Edie Rose to find looks that are sweet and slightly retro, pulling archival references (or full-on vintage) pieces that give her a distinctive edge.

With a commanding name like Guitarricadelafuente, the Spanish singer and actor almost has to have a bold sense of style to match. And he certainly does: The star, who is garnering early Oscar buzz for his role in this year’s La Bola Negra, has been making the press rounds in striking looks all masterminded by stylist Luca Guarini. His casual little Marni V-neck sweater at the GQ Men of the Year Awards! His sleek black Dior tuxedo at the Governor Awards! Get you a man that can do both.

When you’re playing a Disney princess like Moana, your red carpet style has to be just as enchanting—and Samoan-Australian actor Catherine Laga’aia understood this assignment fully. While promoting her live-action reboot of the beloved franchise, the actor and her stylist Alexandra Mandelkorn embraced the tropical, beachy feel of the film—with lightweight summery frocks that struck the right balance of red carpet appropriate yet utterly effortless. From the gauzy white laces to the summery polkadots, her cheery style is a breath of fresh air.

From Not Suitable for Work to season three of The White Lotus, we could simply not escape Nicholas Duvernay on our TV screens this year—not that we’re complaining about it. The star and his stylist Avo Yermagyan have subverted menswear codes to make the silhouettes and details just a touch more intriguing. A three-buttoned tan blazer from DSquared2? Check. A plaid Wooyoungmi suit with a pop-of-red shirt? Check. Serious suiting swagger? Check-check.

#6668. “Two Girls Who Speak All the Time About Politics”: Tao Okamoto and Virginie Efira Take On Capitalism in All of a Sudden

Okamoto and Efira shared the Best Actress Award at Cannes, where All of a Sudden premiered this summer

We’re all seeking comfort as the world ends. Environmental, economic, and political pressures weigh heavily on our minds as tangible solutions feel farther and farther out of reach. Solace is a rare commodity in a world controlled by unrelenting capitalist forces. In All of a Sudden, filmmaker Ryusuke Hamaguchi suggests that as we face tragedy, we must remember our vital need for human connection.

All of a Sudden tells the story of two women who forge a formidable friendship as they face personal and professional hardship. Marie-Lou Fontaine (Virginie Efira) runs an elder-care facility near Paris, where she introduces a “Humanitude” methodology designed to treat patients with dignity and introduce listening-heavy caretaking practice. She befriends Mari (Tao Okamoto), a terminally ill theater director from Japan. Ryusuke chronicles this relationship through extended, emotional conversations, spoken in both Japanese and French, and covering topics from identity to mortality.

The film is an adaptation of a nonfiction book, When Life Suddenly Takes a Turn: Twenty Letters Between a Philosopher With Terminal Cancer and a Medical Anthropologist, which collects correspondence from two Japanese-speaking academics as they reflect on health care and death during the last few months of philosopher Makiko Miyano’s life (who inspired Okamoto’s character). Instead of keeping the fact that the two pen pals spoke the same language, he introduced French and moved the story to Paris. This small change forced the story to confront language gaps, exploring the power of conversation and listening and asserting that so much can be achieved through this mediation.

Efira and Okamoto understand their characters’ simmering anxieties and outlooks on the world, providing the bedrock for these impressively naturalistic performances. The two actresses sustain long, philosophical conversation with such intensity throughout the entire three hours and 16 minutes. In a rare occurrence, the two shared the Best Actress Award at the Cannes Film Festival, where the movie premiered this summer. In the film, their budding friendship serves as a sounding board for each other, as Marie-Lou grapples with the pressure of capitalism on her medical staff and Mari comes to terms with the end of her life. In typical fashion, Ryusuke lets the camera linger on these two actresses during these prolonged philosophical interactions, forcing the audience to sit with the gravity of their situations.

Ahead of the theatrical release of Ryusuke’s latest feature film, Bazaar spoke to Efira and Okamoto about the first time they read the script, how they built an intimate bond despite speaking two different languages, and the punk, anti-capitalist edge fueling this intimate, conversation-heavy film.

Tao Okamoto: It’s the scene where she talks about capitalism while writing on the whiteboard. That’s one of the strangest scenes in the movie. I felt connected to the character because I am also a climate activist myself. I’ve been spreading the word about climate crises on podcasts, and I talk about it daily. When I read the part, I felt, “I need to play this character.”

Virginie Efira: It’s the same for me, because this scene is so special. When I read it, the movie felt like one of the most profound, special, and radical readings. You have two girls who speak all the time about politics. We don’t see that. I never see that in other movies. Sometimes, when a director wants to put something philosophical, political, or intellectual, they say, “Maybe we’ll do three minutes,” otherwise the audience will be bored. No, this movie spent 15 minutes [discussing capitalism], and I said, “Oh yes, that’s so punk!” The film has its own language. When I read All of a Sudden, I could hear the language of the movie, and I wanted to approach it. When I met Tao, I thought, “Oh, we are so lucky to be an actress and work with [Ryusuke], but also to share this material with him.”

VE: I only knew one word in Japanese before making the movie. Then, to be able to speak Japanese at a high level, because the character studied in Japan, I must first learn to read, then learn to embody the language. Finding the language of the movie was strange. There’s a flat and natural way to play [in one of Ryusuke’s movies]. He spoke to me about Cassavetes and Gena Rowlands, but also about Bresson. Neutral performances. You find it when you open up, and when I opened to Tao, we discovered the right language for the movie. We did a lot of flat readings before shooting. We never rehearsed in motion, so when we finally performed for the first time, we awakened the text.

TO: I’m going to add that because I started my career in America, finding a middle ground by using a language that’s not my mother tongue is normal for me. On the surface, that part wasn’t a challenge for me. Finding the language for this film and respecting Hamaguchi’s way of working were priorities. We were naturally drawn to his talent and wanted to make his dream happen and be part of it.

TO: I joined this project way after Virginie. I luckily had months to prepare with him, and during rehearsals, you drop all emotion and read the text as if you were reading numbers. On top of that, I got to visit some institutes, such as the Cancer Research Center and places where people work with disabled people, to build up my understanding of my role’s point of view. Reading the text over and over was a unique experience for me. [Ryusuke] can really listen to the actor’s voice and tell the difference between someone who is simply reading and someone really concentrating. Even though you’re not supposed to put any emotions, you have to be present; you have to be there. I’ve never experienced such rich, profound preparation for a role.

VE: We shot in a real nursing home. There was a mix between fiction and reality. Sometimes filmmaking becomes standardized, with no room left to breathe, but with Hamaguchi, you’re sure he will leave room for the unexpected and for uncertainty. It allows you to embrace the unpredictability of reality. He’s not looking for an accident, but for the ability to be in the present. A viewer of Hamaguchi’s work will always feel a sensation of documentation, but it’s still always cinema. To be an actor in his movies is to be naturalistic, to be in the present, to capture some details and really embrace this unpredictability. The filming process becomes an adventure he wants you to have. One day, he told me, “I hope that you will find the light.” He said a lot of cryptic things. He said to me, “Don’t use your text like a tool; just go inside the text.”

TO: The script is already amazing. And I could read it over and over again, and that was a joy. But he mentioned that I should read the original book. It’s about two women exchanging letters—or emails. They are real people who the characters are modeled after. I wanted to please the people who know these women, not to make them too different from them. I first put pressure on myself to portray this woman as close to the real person, but it was impossible for me because this person passed away in 2019. I couldn’t do much research, so I interviewed her mother and the co-writer. That provided me with a lot of clues, but reading their exchanged letters already gave me the soul of this movie.

VE: He gives the book to the actresses, but also to the entire team. I never felt something so collective, and you will feel it in the movie, from the sound engineer to someone who only stayed two days on set. I also met the anthropologist. When you read this book, it’s full of life. It gives you a perceptible beauty of things. The book has a kind of energy; it helps you keep a level of optimism even when you know the situation is hopeless. In this book, it speaks about what it’s like to be alive. Maybe there’s beauty in life because we are going to die.

TO: For me, I came on this project at the last minute, only a month before. Virginie was so dedicated to studying Japanese from scratch; it was so impressive how she studied all this writing, reading, and lines. Seeing that, I had a huge admiration, like “Who can do this!?” As you can see, Virginie’s so charming; nobody would hate her. It was so easy for me to be drawn to her as a person, as the characters in the movie were discovering each other.

VE: We got to know each other through the shoot. I was happy not to know much at the beginning and to progressively get deeper into our relationship. We lived all that together. I conflate Marie-Lou’s feelings for Mari with Virginie’s feelings for Tao, because we share that. It will be an end, not a tragic one like in the movie, but it will be an end. But I know Tao will carry this experience in her heart forever, and I will too. He let us feel what we want to feel.

TO: I study environmental issues, and I always thought capitalism is responsible for our world’s issues. Something I didn’t know until I read this script was that capitalism doesn’t only exploit our environment, but also our human bodies—human labor and our time. When I connected those dots, I realized all the problems could be blamed on capitalism. We’re looking for time and looking for happiness—or security—and all these things can be related to a capitalistic way of living. I think it’s great that Hamaguchi connected that fundamental issue to Marie-Lou’s situation in the elderly home. She’s frustrated, as is Marie. She’s battling her cancer, and it can be connected to this economic issue.

VE: Cinema can show bodies, fatigue, and with Marie-Lou, you see a certain fatigue because capitalism creates it. How do we deal with that? We say, “Oh, capitalism’s not good. We don’t have time. And we want to be richer and richer.” But how do we fight that, because everything is already there? I come from France, and you see all the young people outside. The real question is, what can cinema do with that? It’s not a theoretical thing, but Hamaguchi can find a solution. It’s speaking, listening to the other, sharing ideas; it’s movement. If I look for a solution to this problem with money, I’ll remain a prisoner of this way of functioning. Even if you think you’re not in a stage of capitalism, you are.

This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

Winter may be cold, but it’s a great time to go and see the city in action. Tivoli Gardens lights up for Christmas and the city settles into the candlelit coziness of hygge season.

A Copenhagen apartment delivers Scandinavian style up close. Think herringbone floors, tall windows, blonde wood, and a kitchen that’s set up to actually cook in. This year in the US, Black Friday is on Friday, November 27, a day after Thanksgiving. While that’s the official date, many retailers roll out deals throughout November. You can expect the biggest discounts to happen between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday, but be on the look out for retailers to launch sales throughout the entirety of cyber week.

Cyber Monday lands on November 30 this year, the Monday after Thanksgiving. Most brands keep the deals rolling through the week—but that doesn't mean a deal will last all day, so act fast.

Are deals better on Black Friday or Cyber Monday?

Black Friday and Cyber Monday offer equally good clothing deals. Plan for large retailers and more-established brands to offer deals on Black Friday, and smaller menswear boutiques to hold out for Cyber Monday. As a baseline, expect the better Black Friday sales to start at 20% off and go upwards from there. In the lead up to Black Friday, also be on the lookout for the coveted sale on sale, which has become the norm in recent years.

#6656. I Tested Peloton's New, More Affordable Folding Treadmill

In my mind and, I think the minds of many others, Peloton has always been a stationary bike brand. The Bike, after all, was its first product, turning the Peloton name into a catch-all term for at-home cycling that we now hear everywhere, from broadcasts of the Tour de France and Giro d'Italia to television sitcoms. (A running gag online is that Peloton's upscale, soothing video workout content is worlds away from The Office's Dwight Schrute leading a group of stationary riders off an imaginary cliff.)

Nevertheless, Peloton actually has been making treadmills since 2018. The first Tread delivered the same proposition as the Bike: premium hardware that looks good enough to bring out of the basement, as well as access to interactive, instructor-led runs and HIIT classes on a big, immersive screen. Over the years, Peloton has brought improvements to that first Tread: larger screens, voice controls, AI-informed movement tracking for form analysis and coaching.

The new Tread Flex, however, heads in a slightly different direction. It has a simpler belt, simpler speakers, a smaller screen. It's $1,300 cheaper than the next step up, and $4,500 cheaper (!) than Peloton's slat belt-equipped Tread+ Vision. Its affordability isn't even its main selling point, however, because the Tread Flex has a nifty final trick: it folds up to save space.

Could these space and money-saving tactics make the Tread as popular as the Bike? Well, I run nearly every day, and ever since a tester Tread Flex showed up at my door, I've been doing it indoors much more frequently. In my experience, here's what makes Peloton's latest worth considering.

Treadmills tend to have a problem that stationary bikes don't: the nicer they get, the bigger they get. Premium models have larger motors and roomier running platforms. In short, they're heavy. (The Tread+ Vision is a hefty 460 pounds.) The Tread Flex is 170 pounds less, and that's crucial to its ability to fold up, because that feature wouldn't be much of a selling point if it felt like adding a power clean to the end of every run.

In reality, stowing the Tread Flex is quite easy. You just lift up the running deck from the end and push it forward until a hydraulic cylinder locks into place. There's a pin clip to lock it. To drop it down, you push forward on the deck and then on the hydraulic support, then walk it back. At about 45 degrees, the hydraulics take over completely; you can go put on your running shoes while a gentle thump lets you know the deck is back on the ground.

Folding up the Tread Flex drops its area from about 16.5 square feet to half that. (The Tread+ Vision is around 19.25.) Just as importantly, I've discovered, is that lifting the deck brings the machine up onto a set of locking wheels. I've kept mine in a designated corner, but it's so easy to move that it wouldn't be much hassle to wheel it out and lower it for every workout, if your space required it. Get your cardio out of the way, then get your cardio out of the way.

Okay, so folding and moving a treadmill might be a pain if you're using it every day. But I suspect if you're running that often, you're doing some of it outside. I live less than an hour away from the Canadian border, and run on roads and trails five or six times a week all year round. Good layers get you pretty far, and there's a reason why run clubs continue to boom while SoulCycle-adjacent Mile High Run Club closed all its studios this year.

Treadmills are for something else. They're for a warm-up prior to lifting, or for bootcamp-style HIIT workouts that combine sprinting intervals with weight intervals. The prioritization value of time spent doing these doesn't seem to align with the space investment a treadmill requires if you don't have a pool house or big garage. (I have a sun porch-slash-mudroom where I keep firewood and ski boots in the winter and a napping couch in the summer.)

This is how, I think, the Tread Flex makes the ultimate proposition as the ideal home treadmill. A treadmill doesn't replace a usual running routine; it adds to it. On Monday I do my usual seven miles down the road and back on the river trails; on Tuesday I let Andy Speer kick my ass with sprints and kickstand deadlifts. (And, sure, when it's -10° and blowing in late January, I might run inside, now that I have the option.)

None of the above would matter as much if it came at the cost of quality. I've run on hotel treadmills that sound like your grandma's washing machine and feel similar to how they look, i.e., stomping around on hollow plastic. The Tread Flex may not have the cushioned slat belt the Tread+ Vision has, but it's definitely not that.

What it does have is a spec that's right in line with top-notch treadmills. Its max speed is 12.5 miles per hour (a 4:48 mile, in runner's units), a 12.5% max incline grade (but no decline), and a 20-inch by 59-inch running surface that, though not cushioned, feels good to run on. The swiveling screen is nice and big at 21.5 inches, with HD resolution and a touchscreen interface. I particularly like how adjusting speed and incline is done with rolling knobs, which feel much better—and more natural—to engage with than buttons when you're gasping at threshold pace.

On top of that is Peloton's interactive experience: You can take live classes where you can pit yourself against others and get kudos from the instructor. The pre-recorded catalogue includes thousands of classes for yoga, Pilates, and meditation, in addition to strength and the running, cycling, and rowing the company makes machines for.

The Tread Flex also provides personalized training plans, smart pacing guidance based on where you're at, automatically adjusting incline for classes, and of course leaderboards and an entire ecosystem of badges and achievements to earn, if you're into all that. For $50 per year, that is.

Oh, and did I mention it's a good-looking machine? It's sleek; an attractive, soft-edged Z with a minimal screen instead of a board of colorful buttons. Nobody's throwing around the word "console" to describe this thing. That's good; home gym setups deserve different consideration than gym rigs. If images of Crunch Fitness flash through your head every time you glance into the corner, something has missed the mark.

Where Peloton's Tread Vision treadmills are clearly high-end, the Tread Flex toes the line against mainstream consumer models. Its features match up with some of the most popular machines, and its price, while at the higher end of the spectrum, does too. But the Tread Flex gets there with more style, and with Peloton's huge ecosystem of live and archived class content.

So, if we're looking at other treadmills out there, my quick answer is yes. The Tread Flex is the utilitarian Peloton Treadmill, but it's still a Peloton treadmill.

How you answer this question really requires asking yourself a series of other questions first. What do you want a treadmill for? How much do you want to invest? Do you want access to fitness classes—especially ones other than running—and are you okay with the $50/month subscription fee?

Form factor and access to classes and content are non-negotiables. The Tread Flex might be Peloton's new entry-level treadmill, but it's far from a simple running machine. Flex refers to that nifty fold-up feature, but also to this treadmill's ability to integrate into an exercise program that also includes strength training, HIIT workouts, yoga, and on and on.

As a runner who prefers to log miles outside whenever possible, I was encouraged by how much I enjoyed running on the Tread Flex. The classes are fun, and Peloton's instructors are real pros, but even in Just Run mode, the Tread Flex proved responsive and comfy. It's getting dark around 4:30 PM these days, and my daylight windows for running on the well-used roads around me have narrowed like a Death Star trash compactor. It's nice to know I can snag seven miles after sundown if need be.

Well, if you aren't limited by space or cash, the Tread Vision and Tread+ Vision get you bigger screens, AI-enabled running form feedback and coaching, and a more cushioned, broader running area. If you just prefer running or walking on a treadmill to doing it outside, investing more heavily in a treadmill is worth considering (though the Tread Flex will still be great).

The Tread Flex's real competition is the NordicTrack Commercial 1750, which you'll find recommended on just about every treadmill buying guide on the internet. The machines are similar in function and specs, but there are some differences. The NordicTrack's running surface is two inches wider and one inch longer; it has a slightly more powerful motor; it can decline to -3% grade; its belt is slightly cushioned; it has a built-in fan; and NordicTrack's class and entertainment platform, iFit, is cheaper at $39 a month.

In comparison, the Tread Flex takes up slightly less space, has a higher max speed (12.5 mph over 12 mph), a steeper incline (12.5% over 12%), and a larger screen (21.5 inches over 16 inches). The rolling knobs to adjust speed and incline are nicer to use. My partner, who designs commercial and residential interior spaces, agrees with me that the Tread Flex is a better-looking machine.

List price for the Tread Flex is $300 cheaper, but the NordicTrack seems to be perpetually on sale. So it might come down to looks, that 3% decline, or what class platform you'd like to buy into.

The actress is embracing a more intentional beauty routine with a little help from RéVive Skincare.

Though her recent red-carpet looks may beg to differ, Brittany Snow is no longer chasing perfection—at least when it comes to her appearance. Instead, the actress, who turned 40 this year and is starring in one of the moment’s most deliciously bingeable series, now in its second season, is focused on aging well and nourishing her skin with intention. “There’s something really freeing about realizing you don’t need to look perfect to feel confident,” Snow says. “I spent so much of my younger years unfortunately being aware of how I looked. Now, I’m much more interested in just looking like myself, just hopefully a little more hydrated.” That’s where RéVive comes in.

Snow credits her makeup artist Charlie Riddle with introducing her to the luxe skin care brand and helping her evolve her relationship to beauty. “He has always focused on making my skin look like skin—healthy, hydrated, and luminous,” she says. “He understands that the better you take care of your skin, the less you need to cover it up.”

Throughout the current press tour, Riddle has been prepping Snow’s skin with RéVive; the brand has quickly become a staple in her personal routine, too. “I was initially drawn to how beautiful my skin felt when Charlie used the products on me,” she says. “There was this sense of hydration without feeling like I had a million things sitting on my face. Charlie has taught me that the edit matters; I used to be someone who thought more products meant better results, and now I realize that consistency and quality are much more important.”

In addition to the products’ elegant feel and innovative, science-based formulas, Snow also appreciates RéVive’s brand story. “RéVive was founded by a plastic surgeon whose research began with helping burn victims heal,” she says. “There’s something really meaningful to me about a beauty brand that was born out of wanting to help people.”

Whether she’s preparing to film a scene, gearing up for a marathon press day, or decompressing before bed at home, she relies on RéVive’s Renewal Moisturizing Night Cream and Renewal Rescue Elixir Oil to hydrate, care for, and rejuvenate her skin.

Both products are powered by exclusive peptides enhanced by RéVive RVGF Technology—a breakthrough delivery system that targets skin concerns with greater precision to maximize efficacy. The complementary formulas work to renew skin overnight to reveal a healthier-looking, more radiant, and glowing complexion by morning.

“My skin goes through so much between filming, travel, and wearing makeup for hours,” she says. “By the end of the day, I really want something that feels rich and helps my skin look refreshed. After using them, my skin feels like glass.”

Glowing from the inside out, her recent appearances—be they in character on our TV screens or in late-night talk show clips on our phones—are proof both of RéVive’s results and the confidence that comes from feeling good in one’s own skin.

#6652. 28 Nordstrom Black Friday 2026 Deals That Go Harder Than Expected

We’re as stoked as the next guy to start chowing down on some turkey and Thanksgiving sides, but the Nordstrom Black Friday sale is looking like the perfect distraction until Thursday comes.

That’s because, as always, the famed department store is your ideal all-in-one stop for any style need—a dapper new suit, a pair of comfier kicks, some killer watches. But these days, it’s also the place to lock in your new skincare routine or find a scintillating cologne, not to mention a whole new kitchen full of Michelin-starred gear and practically a full-on home renovation with luxurious bedding and tasteful decor. All that and more are on offer for the Nordstrom Black Friday sale, and we’ve looked through the entire thing to surface some truly gloat-over-Turkey level deals.

Want more savings intel? Start with our guide to the best Black Friday clothing deals, then make moves to GQ's all-in-one master list of every Black Friday deal that matters.

Whether you need a new suit for the holidays, a pair of boots to get you through Snowmageddon, or a head-to-toe closet refresh, Nordstrom’s got it all discounted. That goes doubly for Veilance's incredible, rain-defying outerwear. We don’t expect that to last long.

Accessories are the bits and bobs that really make your outfits pop. Whether it’s the watch on your wrist, the beanie on your head, or the duffle you carry on your travels, no detail—or discount—is too small.

Like Forrest Gump’s momma always said “you can tell a lot about a person by their shoes.” Whatever it is you want to telegraph to the world, there’s a shoe for you. Prep your feet for winter with a honkin’ pair of boots or pick up a new daily driver like a workhorse pair of derbies. Or maybe get a jump on your marathon training with a new pair of running shoes.

Whether it’s the scruff on your face or the scent you wear, grooming sets your ambiance and aura. That’s crucial if you expect to interact with anyone up close. So pick up a fresh new cologne or get your skincare routine locked down because you’ll never know who you’ll run into.

Even if you end up staying inside without seeing anyone, your home is your sanctuary. Whether your main hangout is the kitchen, the couch, or the bed, Nordstrom can make you feel even more at home with its wide range of deals on bedding, decor, kitchenware, and more.

This year in the US, Black Friday is on Friday, November 27, which is a day after Thanksgiving. But if not obvious already, retailers (like Nordstrom) tend to launch “early” sales to help you get a jump on shopping. And before you ask, the deals are just as good.

Cyber Monday falls on Monday, November 30. Note that most sales will extend through the end of the week, but that won’t be a given.

What are the best things to buy at Nordstrom?

Nordstrom is a legacy department store, so they’ve got you covered for just about everything. But if you’re probably thinking about clothes, specifically. We think that some of the best things to buy at Nordstrom are shoes, suits, and grooming products. Nordstrom also has a surprisingly good amount of designer and niche brands on their roster—you just have to dig through the generic in-house labels to find them.

While there’s no official word on a Nordstrom Cyber Monday sale, our coverage over the years tells us that there most likely will be. We’ve got our ears to the ground and will be updating this story as we hear more.

#6649. How Women Weavers Are Preserving Indigenous Amazigh Culture in Morocco

Malika Oubzou is sitting on a red and blue handwoven rug on the floor of her childhood home in Tamda Noumercid, a small village near Azilal in Morocco’s Atlas Mountains. The 36-year-old weaving artisan is enjoying a glass of milk and a plump, juicy date from a large plate she’s set out for guests—myself among them—when she looks up to see even more people arriving. To accommodate the new visitors, she finishes her milk, leaves the room, and returns with a low table. Then another. And another after that.

Soon enough, more food comes out: a steaming clay pot of tajine maazi (goat tagine) with potatoes and carrots, fresh tomato salad, and fluffy Tafarnout bread, still warm from the clay oven. Malika shifts the tables around to make room for the additional food, and her brother, Mohammed, rearranges the pillows that line the rug-filled floors of the space. It continues like this for the next couple of hours: A table appears here, a pillow moves there. Food comes in and food goes out. The only thing that stays put? The rugs themselves.

Malika Oubzou greets her neighbors at the door of her home in Azilal. In Morocco, Friday is celebrated as "Couscous Day," a cherished tradition where families gather for a communal lunch, usually after the weekly congregational prayer.

“In a typical rural Moroccan household, everything is mobile except the rugs,” Jihane Lahbibi, the Moroccan co-founder of the Moroccan rug brand Casa Amar, tells me as we dunk our Tafarnout into the tagine juices. “The pillows, tables, mattresses…they are all roving. But the rugs are the constant. Symbolically, they are the pillars. They anchor the room. They are the room.” In fact, as Malika echoes later through a translator, rugs are the most sacred part of the home. “When you welcome guests,” she says, “the rug is everything.”

Malika was the first weaver Jihane and her Italian husband Matteo met when they began looking for artisans to make custom rugs for Casa Amar back in 2021. Today, they partner with women in five communities across Morocco to create and source rugs for clients across the world, and were even part of Milan Design Week last year. As interest in Moroccan craftsmanship and design continues to soar, I’ve come to spend some time with a few of the artisans Jihane and Matteo work with to learn more about the Amazigh weaving culture behind the craft.

This scene with the roving tables is a very good start. It’s impossible to miss the deep significance of rugs in everyday Moroccan life once you experience their starring role in every room, after all. But as the days go by, I realize rugs have taken on even more meaning in recent decades, too: They’ve become a way to keep Amazigh culture alive in the face of modernization.

“Younger generations aren’t making as many rugs these days, so when the older women weavers eventually die, the younger ones won’t know how to make them—and that makes me really, really sad,” Malika tells me after we’ve finished our tagine and have moved on to mint tea and a bowl of grapes for dessert. “So now, when I’m weaving, I think about my culture. I also think about the satisfaction of making something good, and the money I will get from making it. All of those things are important. But rugs are objects that last, and because they last, they are one of the best ways to preserve the culture.”

Like most Indigenous traditions around the world, Moroccan rug weaving dates back thousands of years. Amazigh women (also known as Berber) in the Atlas Mountains originally crafted handknotted rugs from local sheep’s wool to protect themselves and their families from the elements: harsh sun during the day, and freezing mountain temperatures at night. Over time, rug weaving morphed into an art form as well, one filled with all sorts of storytelling and symbolism. Some rug patterns represent universal emotions like love and hope, while others are more like talismans, meant to protect against evil and infertility. No matter the pattern, though, the weaving tradition itself has never been written down anywhere. It’s passed down from mother to daughter simply by watching.

Nejma Oubzou prepares freshly harvested dwarf palm by cutting the thorns off and separating the fan-like leaves in order to dry them out. The fibers are used to create woven items such as baskets, mats, and home decor.

“Amazigh women know how to make rugs the same way many other people around the world know how to make bread…it’s just a part of the culture from a very young age,” Jihane, who grew up in Casablanca, tells me one afternoon as we’re driving through the mountains. “It’s not like someone sits you down on the loom and says, ‘This is how you do it.’ It’s just that you learn the same way you learn how to walk: No one tells you, you just learn it by seeing.” When she started Casa Amar in 2021 after leaving her job as a business lawyer, she used to ask the artisans she met when, exactly, they learned to weave for the first time. But now she’s come to understand that seeking out that information was always a fool’s errand. “I realize now that it was never so specific,” she reflects. “It was always: They’re around, they see, and they try.”

That’s exactly what happened with Malika. She wove her first rug at age 15 after years of watching her mom weave, and then watching her weave some more. But that first rug she ultimately created wasn’t just a result of growing up around looms; it was a way for her to care for her own mind. When she was 10, her older brother asked her to drop out of school. Their sister had just gotten married, their parents worked outside the home in agriculture, and he and his younger brother wanted to stay in school—so he decided Malika would be the one to stay home and handle the household chores. Weaving became her creative outlet as a result. “What happened was that after I finished my household work, I had this emptiness that I wanted to fill, and weaving was how I filled it,” she tells me. “I didn’t go to school and I didn’t work, so weaving was how I took care of my brain. I used it to fill a void.”

Today, Malika continues to weave to fulfill her creative dreams, and to make money by doing so. She works independently in the home, not as part of one of the thousands of weaving cooperatives scattered throughout Morocco. When she’s weaving a custom rug for Casa Amar, she follows the design given to her by their clients. But when she’s weaving just for herself or her family (which is increasingly rare due to her growing amount of paid work), her patterns are instinctive and intuitive, usually based on how she is feeling in the moment. “There’s no particular reasoning behind so many of my designs; it’s just what I like and what my mind tells me to do,” she explains. “It’s a very free process. It’s not like if you have green, you have to put yellow. You can do whatever you want. It’s all in the mind when you’re making a rug for yourself.”

But aside from earning a living and expressing her creativity, there’s a third reason Malika weaves: a desire to preserve her craft in the face of modernization. This is where things get slightly complicated because, in some ways, the tradition is thriving. As any design aficionado knows, the allure of Moroccan textiles is increasingly global and well-documented, everywhere from Instagram to the pages of this very magazine. According to the international research firm 6W, the Moroccan rug market is projected to reach $485 million in the US by 2032, up from $371 million in 2025.

Every step of the wool preparation process is done by hand. After the wool is sheared from the animal, the artisans wash, brush, and spin it into yarn.

New York-based interior designer Sarah Lederman believes this uptick in interest could be a response to, take a guess, AI. “People are craving more handmade items in their homes now because they’re the opposite of uniform,” she says, “and Moroccan rugs bear the mark of the person who made them.” They’re a reminder, in other words, of what it means to be human.

Khadija Rhandouss in the carpet section of the weekly souk in Khmisset. Rhandouss is a local businesswoman who trades in Moroccan rugs. Every Tuesday she attends the weekly souk in Khmisset where all the best rug deals happen before sunrise.

At the same time, there are threats to the longevity of traditional rugmaking. For one thing, as Malika mentioned at multiple points throughout my visit, fewer young women are actually learning the traditional weaving techniques required to make said rugs. The work is time-consuming, after all, and the money isn’t always great. And now that there are more profitable career options available elsewhere, many younger women are choosing to leave their villages in the mountains, making weaving less of an obvious path than it once was.

Nejma Oubzou spins wool into yarn at her home in the Atlas Mountains in Morocco.

That’s not to mention the modern technology that has changed the game even more. In the early 2000s, some Moroccan small producers started to buy machines from China that allowed them to process bad-quality wool (known locally as “dead wool”) to make carpets. While starting a new rug used to begin with cutting pure wool from sheep, these machines—which are still used by many today—make it easy to cut out that step entirely. This eliminates a huge and significant part of the process. “A lot of people think that making a carpet is just about weaving on a loom, but actually, making the raw material—i.e., transforming it from sheep to the wool that allows you to start weaving—is just as important,” Ibrahim Noubl, a longtime Moroccan rug dealer, told me in Marrakech at the beginning of my trip. He owns Soufny Art Gallery on the edge of the medina, and often collaborates with the beloved, art-filled hotel El Fenn just a two-minute walk down the road. “In Morocco, we are very sentimental people. We believe in lots of non-material ideas, like the thought that wool is blessed,” he explained. “When blessed wool is inside your home, it will bring you comfort and joy—but all of that disappears when it’s not alive in the first place.”

Mimouna Fadil attaches the wool to a wooden plank to start a new rug at her home in Khmisset.

Artisans, particularly from the Amazigh communities, hand-dye the wool using traditional techniques, often boiling it with ingredients to create long-lasting, eco-friendly colors. Red wool in Moroccan rug making is traditionally achieved using natural dyes derived from plants, minerals, and insects to produce vibrant, lasting colors. Earthy reds often come from henna or madder root, while brighter shades are created with pomegranate peels or cochineal insects.

With that in mind, vintage rugs are one of the best bets for high-quality wool, Ibrahim advises, because the product has already survived a few decades—so you know the wool is good. (Carpets made from “dead wool” often start to smell after a few years.) But to keep the ancient traditions alive in a competitive marketplace, companies like Casa Amar, Salam Hello, and the ever-popular Beni Rugs also sell new rugs and put traditional, sustainable craftsmanship front and center. Not only do they use high-grade natural wool (no “dead wool” to be found here), but they also work directly with artisans like Malika, helping provide an income that allows them to continue their traditional and beloved craft.

Nejma Oubzou, mother of Malika, in her bedroom in her home in the Atlas Mountains. Her name means “stars.”

Many of the artisans even pray before they sit down at the loom because it’s such a sacred act. They start with the Arabic phrase “Bismillah,” which means “in the name of God,” then follow it up with a prayer for peace and serenity during their time on the loom, often including phrases like nsaliw l mensej f salam ou l hna: “We started with peace; may we finish with peace.” After all, as Jihane tells me at various points over the course of our week together, a rug can be both sacred and a source of income. The two are not mutually exclusive. “To buyers, rugs may be just random objects, but people pray before making them, even for people they don’t know,” she says one Friday over Friday couscous, a longtime weekly tradition in Morocco. “I never want to romanticize weaving, because at the end of the day, artisans make the rugs to survive. But both can be true. Just because you have to earn money doesn’t mean you don’t make it respectfully the way your elders did it. It’s something you do with dignity and pride…something to carry the legacy.”

For the last leg of my Morocco trip, Jihane takes me to Khemisset, a small market town about an hour’s drive inland from the capital Rabat, where she lives with Matteo and their two (adorable) young sons. Khemisset is known for its surrounding countryside—think rolling wheat fields, fragrant eucalyptus trees, and grazing sheep—plus its Amazigh weaving traditions, particularly its regionally specific palm mats. Not many artisans make these mats anymore except those in the Khemisset countryside and a few others scattered throughout the Atlas Mountains, and they are sadly going extinct as a result—so I wanted to see them before it’s too late. Jihane and Matteo are also trying to help preserve the mats by spreading the word to their customers. “It’s simple: If people know about them and buy them, artisans will keep making them,” she tells me in the car on the drive from Rabat.

Unlike handknotted rugs, these palm mats are woven from dried palm leaves (not wool) and embroidered with colorful wool patterns on top. They typically cost much less than wool rugs because the raw material is cheaper, but they’re equally difficult to make—and a bit harder on the hands. The leaves tend to dry out during the day, even after the artisans boil them for softness and place them in sachets. As a result, the six women I meet—all of whom collaborate with Jihane and Matteo—often weave late into the night when it’s cooler, or in the morning before the sun becomes too strong. Despite these challenging conditions, they love what they do and are determined to keep the craft alive. (Not entirely unrelated, they are also determined to stuff me and Jihane with more dates, milk, Tafarnout bread, olive oil, and honey—the welcome spread of choice throughout our journey.)

Nora Rhandouss, Khadija Rhandouss, and Jihane share mint tea in Khadija’s salon in Khmisset.

“The techniques to make these mats are very old and very ancestral,” 60-year-old Fatiha Amalou, one of the artisans, tells me as we snack on a bowl of particularly glistening dates. We are sitting on a green and white patterned rug on the floor of another artisan’s house, where we’ve all gathered to chat. Not surprisingly, we’re also circled around a low table that, wouldn’t you know, magically appeared when we arrived. “The mats are so sacred that back in the old days, when people would die, we would wrap them up in them to take them away for burial,” Fatiha continues. “They were like a cape.”

Today, she is dedicated to preserving that sacred weaving tradition. But she also cares deeply about the craftsmanship itself. “Of course I want the legacy to continue; everyone wants the legacy to continue,” she tells me. “But really, perhaps more than anything else, I want to make something that makes me proud. We always say: If you make a good thing, it means you have a good head.” Another artisan, 51-year-old Khadija Rhandouss, nods in agreement. “When I make something good, I feel at peace,” she says. I tell them all that, as a bit of a perfectionist myself, I can relate to that sentiment wholeheartedly. Fatiha just laughs and smiles. “Yes, weaving is what we need to do to make money,” she says, “but it’s also part of what we do to feel good. It’s part of who we are.”

#6646. Thankfully, Omega and Swatch Aren’t Done Making Snoopy MoonSwatches

Four-plus years into the massive collaboration between Omega and Swatch, the partners are still finding ways to reimagine their blockbuster MoonSwatch. And despite nearly 40 iterations of the piece, they still generate massive excitement. The most recent version required interested collectors to fill out an “Electronic Swatch Timepiece Application” in hopes of being selected to purchase one. More than 1.2 million people happily played along. Now, Swatch and Omega are back and playing the hits with a Snoopy-inflected version of the MoonSwatch.

Meet the new Mission to Earthphase - Silver Snowflake. The blacked-out watch is reminiscent of the collector-favorite Speedmaster known as the “Dark Side of the Moon” from 2013. What that watch was lacking compared to this one is an adorable drawing of Snoopy and Woodstock dressed as astronauts and a special silver disc with a unique laser-engraved snowflake design. Safe to say, Omega and Swatch have another hit on their hands.

The black-on-black-on-black design works to great effect here. Everything is rendered in the dark shade: the case, bezel, dial, and matching rubber strap with Velcro closure. Like all MoonSwatch references, the Silver Snowflake model measures 42mm in diameter and features the asymmetric design familiar to Speedy lovers everywhere.

But it’s the easter eggs on the dial that really make this MoonSwatch stand out. Naturally, there are several hidden details. For instance, check out the miniature skis standing in for the indices at 11 o'clock. That’s a special shoutout to the Apollo 11 50th Anniversary of the Speedmaster. This model also returns to a trick employed by the “Cold Moon” MoonSwatch released last November. That watch and this one feature a snowflake design generated at random, meaning each watch is functionally unique. Here, the snowflake appears on a silver-coated disc in the moonphase complication at 2 o’clock.

At 10 o’clock is Swatch and Omega’s signature MoonSwatch “Earth phase” indicator, which bears an image of the Earth with UV ink-coated oceans set against a starry background. Again, look closely: Switzerland is represented in white, its UV ink glowing green in the dark, while Snoopy and Woodstock, represented below, feature secret details in blue-emission UV ink. Protecting the dial is a box-shaped, bio-sourced crystal with an engraved “S” in the center—a detail familiar to fans of vintage Speedmasters, some of which bore “O”-engraved Hesalite crystals.

Like several other MoonSwatch models in the brand’s now-vast collection, buying the Mission to Earthphase - Silver Snowflake requires navigating certain arcane rules. The first part is simple: it’ll be available in stores worldwide this Black Friday, November 27th. However, following that, your only chance to nab one will be when it’s snowing in Switzerland. (And only until March 20th, 2027.) When it comes to the MoonSwatch, simply buying one has become half the fun.

#6645. Vogue’s Best Dressed List of 2026 Is Live! Here’s How to Recreate Our Favorite Looks of the Year

From the red-carpet heavy-hitters to Hollywood’s next generation of stars and the stylists making it all happen, the honorees on our 2026 best-dressed list all share a love for a great outfit. It certainly helps that we do too—which is why we’re coming in with the cold, hard facts: We’re breaking down their style signifiers, one shoppable piece at a time.

The names on this year’s list range from celebrity street style regulars—see: Jennifer Lawrence—to relative newcomers like actor Sarah Pidgeon and singer Gracie Abrams. Model and CFDA judge Paloma Elsesser and actor Ayo Edebiri both appear for their second year in a row on Vogue’s Best Dressed list.

Ahead, you’ll have the chance to browse through some of the honorees’ best looks of 2026, with a snapshot of the key pieces that made those outfits stand out to us—and in turn, dominate the sartorial conversation at Vogue HQ. Some stars championed CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund nominees early on: Edebiri and Lee both wore Lii for press appearances this year, while Lawrence sported one of Colleen Allen’s velvet house coats with a white tee and slippers on a mild fall day in New York. Others are vintage fiends at heart—Elsesser, who self-styled her Vogue Shopping cover shoot in September—chief among them; her everyday looks comprise a mix of vintage Junya Watanabe and Comme des Garçons and emerging designers.

Below, a snapshot of the wardrobes that make up Vogue’s Best Dressed list of 2026, complete with the key pieces needed to shop their signature looks and make them your own.

A regular fixture in our weekly celeb outfits roundups, Jennifer Lawrence is known for her effortless brand of messy-chic, cool-mom-at-drop-off looks, often centered around a ball cap and a slubby vintage tee. The Row and Khaite are mainstay labels in rotation, though, let the record show that she loves mixing more eclectic pieces—like her Colleen Allen velvet house coat—with simple basics (Leset is noted a go-to).

Sarah Pidgeon’s debut on Vogue’s Best Dressed List comes as no surprise: Since playing the role of ’90s style icon, Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy on Ryan Murphy’s Love Story, Pidgeon has taken method acting to a new level with method dressing. For the majority of her public appearances, Pidgeon has stepped out in pieces reflective of Bessette-Kennedy’s refrained style, like a Yohji Yamamoto dress, a collarless Aflalo leather trench, and an embellished mint green slip from Chanel.

Model and CFDA judge Paloma Elsesser is a modern cool-girl, known for her IYKYK approach to dressing . A champion of emerging designers like the London-based, Central Saint Martins graduate Goyagoma, her eclectic style is typically supplemented by vintage grails from the likes Junya Watanabe and Comme des Garçons. For those who worship at the altar of “quiet luxury,” Elsesser eschews that with bold prints, vivid color, and a style that’s all her own.

Like her repertoire of acting roles (TV: The Bear, film: Clarissa, Broadway: Proof), Ayo Edebiri’s style shows as much range as her career choices—from repping emerging designers like Giovanna Flores in a patchwork dress to Conner Ives in pinstripe suiting (yes, the same Ives whose fur-trimmed coat just broke the internet), to her more mature choices for the red carpet, such as Chanel and The Row. Edebiri doesn’t limit herself to one style or silhouette—she can go from feminine dressing to masculine suiting, just as easily as she can shift into various characters (Pacino, anyone?).

Known for her starring roles in this year’s Toy Story 5, as well as in Tron: Ares, and Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse, actor Greta Lee’s sartorial choices take a page out of her action-flick lineup, albeit, with a fashion-forward twist. A fan of bold color-blocking, Lee has worn CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund winner Lii, as well as a fire-engine red fringed gown by High Sport to the London premiere of Toy Story 5, while making bold fashion choices with Marc Jacobs’s iconic blue sequin strapless top from the spring 2026 collection.

It’s been a banner year for the actress Carey Mulligan—in March, she accepted a royal honor in the form of a CBE (Commander of the Order of the British Empire) from King Charles III for her services to drama. Even at Windsor Castle, she used the opportunity to show up in a royally-fashionable ensemble (one, we might say, was fit for a king!) wearing a jacket and trousers from The Row, accessorized with Jacques Marie Mage sunglasses. Then, for the season two premiere of Beef in which she plays a starring role, Mulligan showed up in a pixelated floral skirt and brocade bustier top from designer Julian Klausner’s fall 2026 collection for Dries Van Noten. Her red carpet looks are a mix of sumptuous color, pattern, and texture, illustrated best in a full Colleen Allen look composed of a ruffled velvet top with a coordinating silk column skirt in sunburnt orange.

Another one in Lii’s fashionable girl-gang, actor Whitney Peak (who stars as Lenore Dove Baird in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping) appreciates a color-blocked ensemble, whether it’s for a magazine launch or a press appearance (the latter saw her in London-based designer Torishéju). Her color palettes skews minimalist—think neutrals punctuated by flashes of red—but the silhouettes she gravitates towards are anything but. Case in point: the knitted black Diotima dress she wore to the Academy Museum Gala in Los Angeles was a maximalist’s dream.

Actor Tessa Thompson has been delivering on the red carpet for years now — and her style only continues to bring the wow-factor, from being a fellow fan of Giovanna Flores’s patchwork dress to Kallmeyer’s tailored suiting. She’s known to love a sharp, structured shoulder, and has a penchant for contrasting a delicate silk dress with a strong leather jacket paired. With her Golden Globes nomination for Hedda, starring in the Netflix thriller His & Hers, and a Broadway debut in Fear of 13, co-starring Adrien Brody, Thompson’s style is one that delivers as much variety and star power as her resume.

Our mother in style, Tracee Ellis Ross’s wardrobe is as bright as her star power. With this year’s Broadway debut in Every Brilliant Thing and a daytime Emmy for her show, Solo Traveling, she stepped up her style game even further, with the help of her stylist Law Roach. The Girlfriends and Black-ish star has been experimenting with color and texture as of late, stepping out in highly-saturated ensembles that span an embellished Prada skirt and button-down (look 22 from the fall runway), a marigold tasseled gown by Balenciaga (designed by Pierpaolo Piccioli for spring 2027), and punchy Dries Van Noten (look 35, also from SS27).

After returning to the stage this year with a 16-show sold out residency at Paris’s Plénitude Arena, Celine Dion delivered what the people wanted—and so much more. With daily paparazzi shots that showed off her good humor in style, she stepped out in looks that ranged from suede Jacquemus to all-black leather Tom Ford. Quintessential French design, in feather-trimmed Dior and custom Chanel (she wore a gown that was recreation of her 1997 Oscars dress) rounded out this Canadian in Paris’s sojourn.

The former First Lady has been having fun with fashion as of late—donning a Thom Browne suit set for a ribbon-cutting at the Barack Obama Presidential Center one day to a custom Acne Studios skirt printed with a photo of her late mother, Marian Robinson, the next. At the US Open this summer, she wore a red, white, and navy blue striped Chanel dress from the resort 2027 collection.

Ever since the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards, we haven’t been able to get Gracie Abrams as a gothic vision in Colleen Allen out of our minds. The singer has been serving looks long before that though, stepping out in her signature mix of vintage tees, Conner Ives rugby polos and trousers, and an enviable collection of Chanel pumps. Equal parts comfy and stylish, she’s known to wear a quirky mashup of styles and designers.

#6640. Bobbi Althoff on Tradwives, Reply Guys, and Sharing a Bed With Drake

Bobbi Althoff has a baby face and a vocal fry. Her tenor––which you’ve likely encountered in your TikTok feed, whether or not you know her name––is vaguely baritone and sharply deadpan, an oddly melodic gravel on the eardrum. Depending on who you ask, it’s either endearing, or lazy, or simply slutty. Despite rising to fame on a skittish gaze, the 29-year-old MomTokker turned podcaster turned non-Mormon cast member of Secret Lives of Mormon Wives is now holding eye contact.

We’ve known each other for 20 minutes. She puts down her fork and palms her phone. She wants to read me something, she says, her gemstone-encrusted ring (reading “MOM”) catching the sunlight streaming into The Dominick hotel, where Althoff is staying during the unseasonably warm week of the Mormon Wives premiere.

It’s an essay entitled “I Hate Myself,” written by Althoff when she was a teenager mired in a bout of depression and anxiety made worse by bullies at school. I’d asked what she would title her memoir, if she were to write one, and how she handles online hate, from being accused of sleeping with Drake after interviewing him for her podcast to rumors that her marriage ended due to infidelity to scrutiny about her appearance. “Can a girl gain some weight in her face without you guys fucking saying she has cheek filler?” she wrote on Instagram. “Can a girl be insecure about her upper lip and get some fucking lip filler without you guys fucking commenting on it?” Althoff has been at the center of myriad social media firestorms, some motored by straightforward, internet-enabled misogyny and others by exasperation with her indirect, vaguely hostile approach to engaging with her podcast guests.

She takes a breath, and begins reading. “I want so badly to be able to show everyone the real me, the person that is hurt and is scared to trust anyone, the little girl that is funny, loud, and doesn't care what other people think. Instead of being myself, I create a different personality to satisfy everyone's needs. I hide the real me behind fake smiles and high-pitched laughs.” She pauses, then chuckles (at a normal pitch).

“I was 14 when I wrote that,” she continues. “And that was before ChatGPT. I wrote that myself.”

A smattering of the many awkward—or awkwardly flirtatious—and reliably fury-baiting encounters that have gone down on Althoff’s The Really Good Podcast since its inception in 2023: She and Jason DeRulo LARP a date that gets interrupted by an attempted larceny. While next to him in bed, she informs Drake that Aubrey is a girl’s name. She accuses Michael Cera of founding Cerave, then argues with him about whether his wife needs to know that their feet touched. Lil Yachty threatens to teach her to dance. An oral mishap cum Freudian slip—did she say magician or musician?—in a conversation with Sukihana appears to spark a feud, but instead jumpstarts a friendship and another podcast, this year’s surprisingly raw and affectionate That’s BS with Bobbi and Suki.

Despite her reputation as an invulnerable, even defensive interlocutor, Althoff is strikingly invested in self-exposure. She has spoken openly about her severe struggles with mental illness, insecurities around beauty, her plans to get breast implants, and her painful experience with botched Botox injections. Her penchant for oversharing, she told me, startles her interview subjects, inspiring their own surprising and frank disclosures in return.

“I’m like, hi, nice to meet you, I tried to kill myself,” she tells me. From a young age, she has used comedy to cope with the indignities of womanhood, and she comes by her wry, bluntly charming humor honestly. “Mom, by the time you read this, I’m going to be chilling with Satan,” she remembers writing in a note she left for her mother as a teenager when, she tells me, she attempted suicide. “Keep in mind, I literally was so religious that I accepted that I was going to go to hell for killing myself.” Althoff grew up in a hyper-religious Christian household in California, where she was taught to believe in a classic set piece of Hell that involved “being burned alive forever.”

Althoff has since left the Church, and with it the “conservative worldview” that characterized her adolescence and early adulthood, leading her to get married at the age of 22. Now, she says, she is effortfully de-centering men after “being told that my purpose in life was to be a wife.” Which brings us to her latest venture: divorced, un-religious, founding cast member on a reality show that purports to follow a cabal of Mormon wives living in Orange County. Althoff says her friendships with fellow cast members have been formative and healing, her first experiences with genuine connection among a group of girls after a childhood defined by bullying and a young adulthood spent slaloming down social media slopes riddled with misogynistic vitriol that came from women just as often as it did men.

With her star turn as one of two non-Mormon, unmarried cast members in Mormon Wives, Althoff says she is she surrendering the control over her image that comes with having her own editing team for her podcast, which entails being “completely myself” to a “terrifying” degree. Where the original iteration of Mormon Wives, set in Salt Lake City, centered a pre-existing friend group, the OC spinoff opens on a cast of highly competitive loose acquaintances largely connected by a rabid desire to build their individual audiences. Entering the arena as the most random cast member makes watching Althoff build actual friendships in real-time bizarrely affecting. Instead of sitting safely in the interviewer’s chair, coquettishly crossing her legs and batting her eyelashes, this time those eyelashes are drenched in tears, and she’s not hiding the streaks of mascara dripping down her cheeks.

Those cheeks were once pumped full of Botox, which caused serious facial paralysis (a relatively rare side effect). But enduring a period in which she “couldn’t smile” inspired a shift in her approach to beauty standards and an appreciation for human foibles over cosmetic perfection. “I have been trying to find beauty in the fact that I’m not perfect,” she tells me. “Do I not like my cellulite? Yes, but, I can show it and it’s fine because I’m human. My boobs are saggy: I literally breastfed both of my kids.” Doing reality television also led to an epiphany: she’s been too hard on herself about her appearance. This occurred to her watching the show back with her new castmates-turned-friends, women who she finds beautiful. “I actually don’t need all this stuff,” she says. “I don’t need to have a perfectly chiseled nose and perfect boobs.”

Some might wonder whether joining the Mormon Wives cast, comprised largely of buxom, blonde, traditionally attractive women who in previous iterations of the show have attended group Botox appointments as a form of socializing, might be a counterintuitive way of deprogramming conservative aesthetic norms. But Mormon Wives runs on the tension inherent in its premise: these are women famous for being religious tradwives, who repeatedly slip and fall into subverting tradition: they are breadwinners, they are in bisexual throuples, they talk about sex on camera (even if they insist they only engage in it in the marriage bed). Perhaps most poignantly, they seem to find more emotional sustenance in their relationships with each other than any of their largely deadbeat, cheating, whining, soda-chugging boyfriends and husbands.

In the show’s premiere, she corrects an offscreen producer who calls her an influencer––she’s an internet personality. Online, she is disembodied, cut into clips, context-free and content-forward. And like many of today’s hyper-contemporary internet personalities, Althoff is paradoxically very famous and utterly unknown. As in: she has almost four million followers on Instagram, and every straight man I mentioned this profile to immediately had multiple, highly specific inquiries about interactions she’s had with male celebrities. (“What was it like to share a bed with the 6 God?”) Meanwhile the majority of girls, gays and professional podcasters I brought Althoff up to started at me blankly, evincing not even a dreg of familiarity with her work.

Her legions of followers cannot, in large part, be called “fans,” but do include avid viewers, reply guys, bewildered women, judgmental tradwives, hate-watchers, and pop culture fanatics. She collects connoisseurs more than disciples. As such, Althoff is a cipher, and a harbinger of a novel vector of celebrity that’s potentially liberating for women who’ve been trained to seek validation, adoration, and eternal “relevance,” as she puts it. This makes her an intriguingly modern economic actor. When she is recognized in public, she doesn’t tell her children that they just met a few of Mommy’s fans. “I say, these are all Mommy’s coworkers,” she tells me, seeming sincere as she emphasizes that she wouldn’t want her children to think she was traditionally “famous.” But she clearly can’t resist a facetious acknowledgment of how successful her campaign for relevance has been: “They think I have coworkers everywhere.”

She “judges relevance by incoming brand deals,” which means she’s willing to maneuver to maintain your attention. “My audience has a lot of men who are just wishing they could see me naked,” she says, a reality she enthusiastically “manipulates a little bit.” She knows her combative approach to flirtation sparks outrage among her male viewers. She’s also aware that many of those men resort to infantile insults, which is where her deadpan self-deprecation comes in: “I want to beat people to the punch,” she claims. “You can't call me ugly and have it hurt me because I called myself ugly first. You can't say I'm not funny: I've already said it.”

When I relay to Althoff some of the questions my straight male friends had for her, she admits the rabid speculation around her sex life is frustrating but also flattering. “They obviously think I had a chance with these guests,” she deadpans. “There’s no interaction I can have with a man where people aren’t like, Oh, you guys fucked.” Her haters, she’s observed, fall into two camps: Trump voting white men “who think they would never have a chance with me” and believe unmarried mothers to be morally corrupt. On the flip side are “women who are jealous.”

Her political leanings––which have veered far to the left since her childhood––periodically foment some turmoil among her new girl squad, but Althoff says she also finds much to admire in her conservative cast members lifestyles. “Do I agree with everything in the Church? No. But I see the beauty in the tradwife life.” The relationship between McCall DaPron, a fellow cast member and frenemy turned pseudo sister of Althoff’s, inspired her to break up with her ex, because she saw a healthy dynamic missing from her own relationship. She is committed to maintaining her conviction around political issues her cast members might rather not address: “Does it bother me when I’m the only one in the cast posting about certain things happening in the world? Yes. Fuck ICE, Free Palestine. Free Congo. Free Sudan.”

She hopes her onscreen proto-sister wives, and viewers like them, might allow her to “burst that bubble a little bit”—to widen their perspectives, open their eyes, and inspire re-evaluations of issues close to Althoff’s heart. Admittedly, as the show illuminates, sometimes that means earnestly defending a political position, and other times it means (antifascistly?) refusing to follow the dress code one of the other women attempts to enforce at a party. Observing that male guests on her podcast “always rank themselves a ten out of ten, she notes that “men could be a little more realistic.” She’s not attacking all men, she clarifies, but she would like to alert them to the following: “I don't need to fuck every man that hits on me.”

She adds, with the sprightly sarcasm that’s become her trademark, one final message to readers of this magazine: “Men who read GQ: be nicer to me. I’m not mean, I don’t hate you, don’t hate me.”
