#6639. Ballerina Farm Is Opening a Restaurant, Farm Store, and Cooking School—Here’s a First Look

It’s a glorious late-September morning in the Kamas Valley, and dozens of cows with handwritten name tags are circling me. A soft breeze hints at the seasonal shift that will soon blanket this bucolic corner of Utah in frost. I’m standing beside two of Daniel Neeleman’s daughters and Daniel himself, his head full of curly hair and his feet tucked into work boots. He exudes the easy familiarity of an old friend, despite a family name—and now a social media presence, thanks to Ballerina Farm’s 20 million–plus combined followers—that has taken on a life of its own.

Still, the eloquence and enthusiasm with which he discusses the economics of small-scale agriculture surprise me. “We love small agriculture and the diversification of it,” he says. “I think that we can make an impact in helping people see that small agriculture can work. Whether you’re doing an agritourism aspect or not, we still think it should and can be profitable.”

He speaks about each of the farm’s 120 animals with a fondness that belies his otherwise pragmatic approach to building a modern agricultural enterprise in America. Daniel did not grow up with animals and still remembers how mesmerized he was the first time he saw a cow. “I tell people on the farm tours all the time, if your endorphins are going off watching these animals, watch out. You might be a farmer. It doesn’t go away—it might come back to you later in life.” From the very day that Daniel and his now famous wife, Hannah, bought their first farm in 2017, he knew this was where they were meant to be.

Earlier that morning, I was sitting at their kitchen dining table over a brunch of quiche, greens, yogurt, and tea made from just-picked mint, the spread illuminated by beeswax spindle candles. “It’s our responsibility, and our love and passion too, to build this,” Hannah tells me, wearing a white dress with three daughters by her side. She’s sitting against a backdrop that’s become familiar to millions who have watched her cook and feed her growing family on a farm less than an hour outside Salt Lake City.

Despite their sincere intentions, the Neelemans’ endeavor has brought moments of global controversy. The internet has scrutinized their approach to homeschooling their nine children, their family wealth, and how they balance their roles as parents and cofounders. “We don’t take the platform that we’ve been given lightly,” Hannah says. Agriculture, she explains, has been at the heart of the project from the beginning, even as its reach has expanded far beyond the Kamas Valley. “It has worn a lot of different hats as it’s grown. We were young city kids, and we craved something real and knowing where our food comes from.”

Now, what began as a story told online is becoming a universe people can actually step into. On a stretch of land that spreads out beyond the window like something from “America the Beautiful,” they’re planning—and here announcing—one of the country’s most ambitious new farm hospitality destinations: a cookery school, farm-to-table restaurant, farm store, and spaces for agricultural education and events, all set within a working farm encompassing livestock, organic gardens, a dairy, and a forthcoming creamery.

At the heart of the vision is a cookery school, scheduled to open in 2029, that is as much about learning to cook from the farm as it is about taking those lessons home. The goal is to teach people how to cook seasonally and adapt when certain ingredients aren’t available, wherever they might live. (Daniel describes this as an education in life skills rather than formal chef training.) “I want students to have time with the dairy, the market garden, the creamery, so they’re seeing where the food comes from,” Hannah notes.

The cookery school will be guided by a philosophy similar to that of the legendary Ballymaloe Cookery School, where Hannah and Daniel spent 12 weeks in 2025—and first met Michael “Tiffin” Griffin, a beloved longtime instructor who has since joined Ballerina Farm as the director of the culinary experience. (A more formal, fine-dining restaurant may eventually complement the school.)

But visitors can step into the new Ballerina Farm world as soon as fall 2027, when a Dutch barn is slated to open at the site of the current Kamas market. Inside will be a restaurant and café, which the couple collectively calls an “eatery,” serving meals featuring the meat, dairy, and produce grown on the surrounding farm—a considerable expansion of the current menus at the Midway store and food truck.

Across a breezeway, a market will offer fresh produce straight from the garden and meat and dairy from the livestock—think onions, pea shoots, beets, rib-eye steaks, smoked paprika goat cheese, and gallons of A2/A2 cream-top whole milk—as well as a growing selection of prepared sides, sauces, and meals, from pickled torpedo onions to just-juiced turmeric ginger shots to chicken salad. The latter is Hannah’s particular favorite. “We got so attached to the chicken salad that we had this summer, because we grew meat chickens. We harvested them. And they made the most delicious chicken salad. Then Tiffin told us this week, ‘One more week of the chicken salad—I’m out of pickles. You’ll see it next spring.’ And I went, ‘Nooo.’” She laughs. “I think people are getting back to how grandma used to cook. She cooked from the garden, and it was amazing food.”

Just-cut spinach and radishes will sit next to Ballerina Farm’s signature products, initially available only online, as well as Ballerina Farm’s home goods like oven mitts, aprons, and wooden measuring spoons, with the name appearing only discreetly. They also launched their first skin-care product just this month: Tallow Tin body butter—made with tallow from the cattle, naturally.

The restaurant, farm store, and connecting courtyard will be more than five times the size of the existing Ballerina Farm store and café that opened in 2025, 25 minutes down the road in Midway. “There’s an awful lot of hullabaloo about Hannah doing it, but for me that’s what I saw when I was a kid,” Tiffin, the culinary director, tells me. “That’s how my grandmother lived her life.”

Over a two-hour meal of Ballerina Farm roasted chicken, garden carrots, pickled onions, and homemade yogurt, I sat enraptured by Tiffin’s story and the depth of knowledge and experience that had brought him to this particular farm in Utah. While guests can expect a diversity of dishes—Tiffin is especially passionate about Moroccan flavors—the land is the final decision maker. “We’ll ask Tiffin what’s on the menu for an event,” Daniel explains, “and the first thing he’ll say is, ‘Let me call Madison [Goodman], the head grower.’”

Goodman is responsible for a vegetable operation that will eventually expand to five acres. The kitchen will draw on its harvest but supplement it with neighboring producers when necessary—a philosophy similar to that which guided Tiffin at Ballymaloe: “If we can’t grow it, we get it locally. If we can’t get it locally, we’ll get the best.”

The design and architecture of the project, meanwhile, will be led by Patrick Williams of Berdoulat, the British design house known for its richly textured, historically informed interiors. At Berdoulat, the mantra is “the house rules.” But as Williams puts it, “In this instance, where the buildings are yet to exist, the land rules.” His designs draw inspiration from 19th-century settlers’ homes and agricultural buildings in the Kamas Valley (and, yes, the family’s famous farmstead).

The Ballerina Farm team has worked closely with Kamas officials for years now to define what can be developed on its 14-acre property, prompting the city to introduce new agritourism zoning in 2024. The plans also protect the property’s conserved wetlands. “We are constantly in touch with the city,” says Brad Roberts, the brand’s director of marketing. If done well, Kamas can become a role model for the many other small towns grappling with their own decisions around the opportunities made possible through agritourism.

Yet the Kamas Valley is not the most obvious place to craft such an ambitious project that’s certain to draw travelers not only from the coasts but also from overseas. (Eighty percent of Ballerina Farm’s 10 million–plus Instagram following is based outside of the US.) A high water table can flood the gardens, frosts set in as early as October, and voles relentlessly try to work their way into the harvest. But the valley has a certain quality of light, giant skies, and an openness that feels rarer than ever in today’s world.

Walking through three high tunnels filled to the brim with produce, I eventually met Goodman, a fourth-generation farmer who ran his own successful community-supported agriculture program in the Kamas Valley and was courted for years by the Neelemans before joining the Ballerina Farm team. He speaks passionately about the farm’s recently earned USDA organic certification and the decades of advocacy that brought those standards into existence. “You can make me cry, because there are a lot of people who fought hard for this,” Goodman says, describing the certification’s baseline standards as the floor while emphasizing that he’s reaching for the ceiling. “The label helps us bridge this gap that we, as a society, have created between our reality.”

He continues: “Everything here has a story. I can tell you the story of the winter leek. I can tell you the story of these girls.” (The girls are chickens.) He then spends 10 minutes explaining to me exactly why these chickens—Freedom Rangers rather than the more commonly raised Cornish Cross—are so special and how they’re raised from chicks to harvest. “It’s hard for me to do this and not believe in a creator,” Goodman says.

One of the challenges and opportunities of an agritourism project is that, in a four-season destination like Utah, the experience will be remarkably different depending on when visitors arrive: tomatoes in the summer, spinach in the winter, chicks in one season, and a mature flock in another. “There’s something beautiful about eating what’s in season and retraining us as eaters to appreciate that,” Hannah reflects. “I have started to notice that I’m craving spinach, pumpkin, and squash because your body wants the things that are growing.”

The culture side of agriculture has probably played a larger role in the Neelemans’ agricultural pursuits than they expected, however. While Hannah started sharing on social media as a way to kick-start business for their nascent pork operation, it snowballed into a public inquisition over what many perceived as an idealized, regressive performance of rural domesticity. But what the public wanted to know most was how it was possible. What was real? And who funded it?

When I ask them about balancing their ambitious vision with the realities of building a farm and business, Hannah says, “That’s a true founder of a company. They are the one who has to hold those two worlds together. We have to keep the dreams alive and the fire burning, but we’re also camping over the farm stand or dealing with broken pipes and trying to put up hoop houses.”

Daniel adds: “We’re the ones that decide whenever there’s money left over at the end of the month from the business.” He says that every individual part of the business is profitable. “We don’t have any investors, we don’t have any partners—it’s just us. So then it’s just a question of, What projects are we going to conquer first? We are a for-profit company, and we have to be good stewards of the finances of all the things. It has to be sustainable.”

For years, people have been asking to visit, Hannah explains, sending her messages asking to meet the animals, help with chores, or simply spend a day on the farm. At the time, the Neelemans weren’t equipped to receive this audience of millions who had developed a relationship with a place they’d never visited. Now, they’re preparing to welcome both admirers and curious outsiders, as well as farmers and cooks, into the world that has generated so much conversation. “We have a community that wants to be a part of it,” Hannah recalls thinking. “So how do we build it?”

This new expression of Ballerina Farm places Hannah and Daniel among a lineage of visionaries in farm hospitality who have transformed working farms into gathering places—Ballymaloe, yes, but also Daylesford Organic in the English Cotswolds and Babylonstoren in South Africa. But of course, one important factor sets Ballerina Farm’s journey apart. Rather than building a hospitality destination and then finding an audience, the Neelemans are working the other way around. The relationship is already shaped by years of watching the family’s life unfold online—and by the very different ideas people have formed about what Ballerina Farm represents.

It’s easy to understand the appeal: Rather than watch a 60-second video on their phones, visitors can pull sourdough or slip on a Ballerina Farm oven mitt and slide a pork chop out of the oven. They can greet a just-born calf. Their children can run the fields, breathe the fresh Utah air, and taste the milk from Daniel’s cows. As I pulled through the gates of Ballerina Farm in my rental car and watched six Sebastopol geese waddle in front of me, even I felt that very modern feeling of disorienting familiarity upon experiencing a person or a place in the flesh that I had only ever seen on a screen.

Right now, the Kamas property has already begun hosting farm dinners, seasonal events, and agricultural experiences alongside the market and food truck. Each offering showcases how the Ballerina Farm world will eventually come together: market, meals, events, education, animals, and gardens all in one place.

And for all the ambition of what Hannah and Daniel are building, the idea at its heart remains deeply personal. “The greatest work that we can do is in our homes and our own families and our communities,” Hannah tells me, a conviction that has remained constant even as Ballerina Farm’s audience has rapidly grown.

Adds Daniel, “We’ve accomplished some things that we’re proud of, but we’re far from being done.”

A swipe of lipstick is one of the easiest ways to look instantly put together with minimal effort. Even if you have nothing else on your face, a hint of lip color can lift your complexion. It also works as an accessory or finishing touch for even the simplest outfits.

As we get older, lips naturally feel drier and lose volume. A good balm nourishes and comforts parched lips, but if you want more pigment, many lipsticks are designed for mature skin.

First, steer clear of ultra-matte formulas, as they tend to dehydrate lips and highlight every fine lip line imaginable. They also tend to look flat.

For extra long wear, try a velvety, soft-matte formula instead. It delivers a similar, statement-making finish that's elegant while creating a pillowy, plush effect.

Satin formulas perform well, too. The gentle shine creates the illusion of healthier-looking lips, and it feels less drying throughout the day. That said, brighter shades like reds and oranges can be a little messy to apply, so apply one layer, blend with a fingertip, and blot with a tissue. Repeat to build intensity. If feathering (when the color "bleeds" into fine lines around your lips) is an issue, a clear lip liner around the perimeter should create a barrier.

It's always best to get your skincare benefits from your lip balm, but nourishing plant oils and hydrating ingredients such as glycerin and hyaluronic acid in your lipstick will help maintain hydration as the day goes on.

For makeup artist and Jones Road founder Bobbi Brown, there are no hard-and-fast rules—no matter your age. "It's about your style, what you feel most comfortable in," she tells Bazaar UK.

If you're keen on neutral tones, remember that neutral doesn't mean beige. "Pay attention to what your natural lip color is. I have a slightly bluish-purple tone to my lips. You might have more of a pink tone. It's really great to find a lipstick that really looks like your lips, and the only way is to test it on your bottom lip," says Brown, who notes that a great neutral should not wash you out.

Revered makeup artist Bobbi Brown is no stranger to creating iconic lipsticks. The Classic Lip has all the hallmarks of a modern formula: creamy, intensely hydrating, and richly pigmented. The 12-color range offers enough variety without overwhelming consumers. Expect skin-enhancing neutrals and bolder tones for any occasion.

Trinny London excels at makeup for mature skin, and this recent launch is certainly no exception. It's a glossy, mega-hydrating formula that reflects light beautifully, making lips look plumper, and it's formulated with peptides to help reduce fine lines over time. There's a full spectrum of nude shades, but we love the bold red Poppy for festive nights.

A richly pigmented, buttery-smooth formula that promises to minimize dryness without sacrificing impact. It contains plenty of nourishing oils to keep moisture lasting without feathering into fine lines. It has a rosy scent, so keep that in mind if you're sensitive to fragrance.

Everything Victoria Beckham does delivers instant polish to the lips without extra effort. This slimline lipstick is no exception. It glides on like a tinted lip balm, adding a touch more color while infusing skin with hydration. VB has perfected the art of neutrals, so expect to find easy-to-wear hues for all skin tones. Glide on, then pat to blend any hard edges. It's one of those formulas you won't need a mirror to apply.

Refillable makeup isn't new, but Lisa Eldridge has painstakingly ensured every part of her Rouge Experience lipstick is recyclable, while it still looks like it belongs on a movie star's dresser. The emollient formula glides on like balmy, satin lipstick but won't budge once it sets. Expect long-wear color without the drying side effects.

#6636. An All-Time Great Air Jordan Is Returning on Black Friday

Sit still for a second. The birds are singing. The sun is shining. The Air Jordan 4 ‘Bred’ is returning. Nature is healing. Everything, for once, is exactly where it should be.

The ‘Bred’ (short for “black and red”) is one of the original Air Jordan 4 colorways from 1989. Created by legendary Nike designer Tinker Hatfield, it came in slick black nubuck with hits of gray and red throughout. Michael Jordan famously wore a pair when he hit The Shot over Craig Ehlo to knock the Cleveland Cavaliers out of the 1989 NBA Playoffs—so, yeah, there’s a bit of lore there too.

Unsurprisingly, Jordan Brand has brought it back a few times over the past few years. There was a retro in 1999, followed by versions in 2008 and 2012, and then another in 2019, which finally brought the OG “Nike Air” branding back to the heel. Then, in 2024, we got the ‘Bred Reimagined,’ which swapped the classic nubuck for leather. The less said about that one, the better.

Because two years later, Jordan Brand is going back to the good stuff. The ‘Bred’ is decked out in black nubuck again, with gray eyelets, red accents around the sole, and the all-important “Nike Air” stamped across the back. Even the Nike branding on the outsole is returning. Basically, if you looked at the ‘Bred Reimagined’ and thought, “Look how they massacred my boy,” congrats: this one's for you.

And there’s something quite nice about that. The AJ4 has been messed with, remixed, collabed on, and reworked in just about every way possible over the last few years. Some of those experiments have been great! Some… not so much. The ‘Bred’ doesn’t really need any of that. It’s been one of the best Air Jordans on the planet for 37 years. If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it.

The Air Jordan 4 ‘Bred’ is set to drop on November 27 via Nike, the SNKRS app, and select stockists globally.

#6631. Veruschka, the Shape-Shifting Supermodel Who Defined an Era, Has Died at 87

Richard Avedon famously pronounced Veruschka “the most beautiful woman in the world.” But what made the German model so mesmerizing was her seeming disinterest in preserving any one iteration of that beauty. She could be imperious or impish, feral or feline, androgynous or opulently feminine. She could contort her impossibly long limbs into unreal configurations, traversing fashion magazines and the wider public’s consciousness with ease in a way that had never been done before. One of the original supermodels, Veruschka was also among fashion’s great performance artists.

On November 25 it was confirmed by the German newspaper Bild that the model died at the age of 87, surrounded by friends and family at home.

It was only earlier this month, on the occasion of the release of Ron Howard’s Netflix documentary Avedon, that Vogue revisited an extraordinary 25-page fashion editorial from its March 1, 1967, issue. Across those pages, Veruschka leapt and pirouetted, her hair fashioned into a long, swinging braid by hairstylist Ara Gallant. Avedon had found in Veruschka a woman who could give physical expression to his imagination and whose own imagination was every bit as expansive. Here was a woman whose beauty “demands something, and you must extend yourself to meet the challenge or know that a kind of splendor is lost to you forever,” said Avedon.

Born Vera Gottliebe Anna Gräfin von Lehndorff-Steinort on May 14, 1939, in Königsberg, East Prussia (now Kaliningrad, Russia), Veruschka’s early life was marked by the horrors of war. She was five years old when her father, Count Heinrich von Lehndorff-Steinort, was executed for his involvement in the failed 1944 plot to assassinate Adolf Hitler. The family was imprisoned by the Nazi regime, and the aristocratic world into which she had been born had all but disappeared by the time the war came to an end.

An art student, she was discovered in Florence in 1959. Her early forays into modeling were not immediately fruitful: Standing over six feet tall, she was an unconventional proposition even then. An initial stint in New York proved disappointing, but in Italy she developed a fruitful creative relationship with photographer Johnny Moncada. Some 3,000 images from those formative years, undiscovered for decades, would eventually form the basis of the book From Vera to Veruschka: The Unseen Photographs by Johnny Moncada and an accompanying exhibition at London’s Somerset House in 2014.

Her greatest act of reinvention was, arguably, the creation of Veruschka herself. Adopting the Russian-sounding diminutive of her first name, she cultivated a persona of indeterminate provenance and mystique. Returning to New York in 1964, she found an industry increasingly receptive to her brand of beauty. In Diana Vreeland, then editor in chief of Vogue, she found a kindred spirit.

The 1960s heralded the ascendance of a new breed of model, with the likes of Jean Shrimpton, Twiggy, Donyale Luna, and Penelope Tree becoming cultural figures in their own right. Veruschka, with her high forehead, sculptural cheekbones, and elongated limbs, was one of the decade’s most arresting presences, whatever aesthetic she took on. She appeared on 13 American Vogue covers, working with the likes of Avedon, Irving Penn, Horst P. Horst, and David Bailey, and became one of the highest-paid models of her generation.

Some of her most enduring images were made in collaboration with the Italian photographer Franco Rubartelli, her creative and romantic partner. Among them was the indelible 1968 photograph of Veruschka in Yves Saint Laurent’s lace-up safari jacket for French Vogue, an image that distilled the designer’s new vocabulary of female sensuality and authority.

Veruschka was also an endlessly inventive beauty muse. The Vogue archives are rich with examples of her aesthetic adventurism. She sports fantastical lashes, intricately braided hair, graphic eye makeup, and elaborate headpieces. She was chameleonic, which made her popular with the hair and makeup artists of the era.

And her fame extended well beyond the pages of fashion magazines. In Michelangelo Antonioni’s seminal 1966 film Blow-Up, set in Swinging London, Veruschka played a version of herself in a brief but electrifying scene opposite David Hemmings’s fashion photographer. A year later, she graced the cover of Life magazine. Few models before her had so thoroughly captured the imagination of the wider public, and her legacy lives on in the new generation of celebrity models today.

By the mid-1970s, however, Veruschka had grown disenchanted with the fashion industry. Her artistic ambitions began to take greater precedence over her modeling career. In collaboration with the German artist Holger Trülzsch, she embarked on a captivating body of photographic work in which her painted figure dissolved into architectural surfaces and natural environments, or assumed entirely different identities.

In 1971 Veruschka also appeared in West German magazine Stern with 27 other women under the coverline: “Wir haben abgetrieben!” (“We’ve had abortions!”) to advocate for abortion law reform at a time when it was illegal. It was a significant moment in Germany’s ’70s feminist wave.

Still, fashion never entirely relinquished its fascination with her, nor she with it. There were occasional returns to the runway, including for Chanel in 1994 and, at the age of 71, for Giles Deacon’s spring 2011 show in London. In 2017, Acne Studios enlisted her for its resort 2018 look book. In contemporary photos—with her silver hair slicked back, sporting oversized, louche tailoring—she looks every bit as modern as she had half a century earlier.

Veruschka on the red carpet at the Berlin Film Festival in 2015.

Much has been made of Veruschka’s otherworldliness, but there was something profoundly human in her commitment to metamorphosis. At the height of her fame, she could have made a career out of being the most beautiful woman in the world. How much more interesting, instead, to become a thousand different women.

#6630. What Is Smart Aging? Experts Explain the Skin Care Shift Replacing Antiaging

Hailey Bieber’s preferred term reframes aging as prevention, protection, and smarter skin care.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Beauty terminology has evolved quite rapidly in recent years—particularly around aging. What was long labeled antiaging has shifted toward more realistic definitions of what happens to skin and the body as we get older. But the latest buzzword, longevity, as ubiquitous as it’s become, doesn’t exactly fill the gap for those seeking ways to keep skin, hair, and the body looking youthful. Hailey Bieber’s recent use of the term “smart aging” just may be the word substitute the category has been missing.

Natalia Guzman, FNP-C, CANS, a board-certified nurse practitioner at Atelier Aesthetix in Beverly Hills, explains that smart aging is a proactive, science-based approach to maintaining healthy, youthful-looking skin while embracing the natural aging process. “Rather than trying to ‘stop’ aging altogether, which is biologically impossible, smart aging focuses on understanding how our skin changes over time and making informed decisions to preserve a healthy, strong, overall youthful appearance,” Guzman tells ELLE.

From a dermatologic perspective, Dr. Brianna Olamiju, a board-certified dermatologist with Spring Street Dermatology in NYC, offers this explanation: “Smart aging is about being proactive, making informed skin care choices, and supporting the skin’s natural functions over time. It involves protecting the skin from environmental damage, maintaining a healthy skin barrier, stimulating collagen production when appropriate, and addressing concerns such as fine lines, wrinkles, uneven pigmentation, and loss of elasticity,” says Olamiju. Ultimately, she says, smart aging is about helping your skin look and feel its best at every stage of life while embracing the natural aging process.

Guzman emphasizes that aging beautifully isn’t about looking young. “It’s about looking and feeling like the best version of yourself at every stage of life.”

As skin evolves, collagen production gradually declines, cellular turnover slows, and environmental factors such as UV exposure, pollution, and lifestyle habits contribute to visible signs of aging. Guzman adds that smart aging means addressing these changes strategically through preventative skin care, healthy lifestyle choices, and, when appropriate, evidence-based aesthetic treatments. “I like to think of smart aging as investing in your skin’s future and being proactive rather than waiting until significant changes occur and attempting to reverse them,” Guzman says. “A lot of the time, the latter takes much more work, and sometimes it cannot be completely corrected.”

According to Guzman, the biggest difference between smart aging and traditional antiaging is the philosophy behind it. “For decades, the beauty industry has promoted the idea that aging is something we need to fight, prevent, or erase,” says Guzman. The term “antiaging” often focuses on correcting visible signs of aging, such as wrinkles, volume loss, pigmentation, and skin laxity.

Both Guzman and Olamiju agree that smart aging takes a more holistic, comprehensive, and realistic approach. Olamiju says that anti-aging creates the expectation that we should try to look younger indefinitely. “Smart aging shifts the focus toward skin health, prevention, and maintaining long-term skin quality. Rather than viewing wrinkles, fine lines, and changes in skin textureas something that must be eliminated, smart aging encourages us to support the skin as it naturally evolves. It is less about fighting aging and more about aging well,” she explains. This approach, she adds, also emphasizes consistency, prevention, and individualized treatments rather than chasing every new product or cosmetic trend.

Guzman adds that smart aging, instead of fighting age, means working with the skin’s biology to help it function and look its best for as long as possible. “The main difference is that we’re not simply chasing wrinkles. We're creating a long-term strategy that prioritizes skin quality, natural-looking results, and overall skin health,” Guzman emphasizes. “To me, anti-aging is often about correcting what we see today, while smart aging is about preventing and protecting what we’ll see tomorrow.”

Olamiju and Guzman are completely aligned on the first step in a smart aging routine: wearing sunscreen daily. “The foundation of smart aging starts with a consistent skincare routine and healthy lifestyle habits. Daily broad-spectrum sunscreen with an SPF of at least 30 is arguably the most important step because ultraviolet exposure is one of the leading contributors to premature skin aging, including wrinkles, loss of elasticity, and uneven pigmentation,” says Olamiju. Guzman adds that UV exposure contributes significantly to collagen breakdown and changes in skin texture, noting that sunscreen is essential even on cloudy days.

Olamiju also recommends incorporating topical antioxidants, such as vitamin C, to help protect against environmental oxidative stress, along with moisturizers containing ingredients like ceramides and hyaluronic acid to support hydration and the skin barrier. “Retinoids, including retinol and prescription tretinoin, can be beneficial for improving fine lines, skin texture, and collagen production, provided they are appropriate for the individual,” Olamiju describes.

Bio-Therapeutic bt-sculpt Gen2 Microcurrent Facial Sculpting System

Once your at-home routine is in place, Guzman recommends strategically incorporating preventive and corrective aesthetic treatments. “Depending on the patient’s age, anatomy, and concerns, treatments such as neuromodulators, collagen-stimulating injectables, microneedling, and energy-based devices may help maintain or improve certain aspects of skin appearance,” says Guzman. The key, she adds, is choosing the right treatment for the right patient rather than following every new aesthetic trend. Olamiju includes chemical peels in a very similar list of in-office treatments, depending, of course, on an individual’s concerns, skin type, and goals.

Finally, the experts agree: don’t underestimate lifestyle. Adequate sleep, regular exercise, balanced nutrition rich in antioxidants and healthy fats, avoiding smoking, managing chronic stress, and limiting excessive alcohol consumption all contribute to overall health and can influence how our skin looks and functions.

The best time to start is earlier than most people think, Olamiju shares. Ideally in your 20s, when prevention can have a meaningful long-term impact. “This does not mean that someone in their 20s needs an elaborate skincare routine or aggressive cosmetic treatments. Rather, it is an opportunity to establish healthy habits, including daily sunscreen use, gentle cleansing, and consistent moisturizing,” says Olamiju.

Guzman advises starting a smart aging routine before you feel like you need to correct something, but it’s also never too late to begin. “I encourage patients to think of smart aging as something that evolves with them rather than a routine that begins at a specific birthday,” she adds, offering this decade-by-decade breakdown:

In your 20s. The priority should be prevention. This means establishing healthy skincare habits, wearing sunscreen consistently, maintaining hydration, and introducing targeted active ingredients when appropriate. At this stage, the goal isn’t to aggressively treat aging. It's to protect the skin and build a strong foundation.

In your 30s. You may begin noticing subtle changes in skin texture, fine lines, pigmentation, or elasticity. This is often a good time to reassess your skin care routine and consider professional treatments based on individual needs. It may also be time to consider a little Botox, energy-based treatments, and biostimulators, all depending on the individual’s needs.

In your 40s and 50s. Changes in collagen, facial volume, skin elasticity, and hormonal influences may become more noticeable. A smart aging approach at this stage may include a combination of medical-grade skin care, collagen-supporting treatments, and continued careful selection of aesthetic procedures.

In your 60s and beyond. The focus remains on maintaining skin health, supporting the skin barrier, addressing concerns such as dryness and uneven pigmentation, and choosing treatments that respect the skin’s changing needs.

Olamiju adds that even patients who begin prioritizing their skin health later in life can benefit significantly from consistent sun protection and an appropriately tailored skin care regimen.

Guzman says this is one of the most important conversations we should be having in modern aesthetics. Both experts say smart aging is not a one-size-fits-all concept. They explain that different skin types and skin tones can experience visible aging differently, and understanding those differences is essential to creating a safe and effective treatment plan.

Individuals with lighter skin tones may notice fine lines, redness, and visible sun damage earlier, particularly if they have a history of significant UV exposure. Those with darker skin tones may have more visible concerns related to uneven pigmentation, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and changesin skin tone. “Melanin provides some natural protection against ultraviolet radiation, but it does not eliminate the risk of sun damage or skin cancer, so daily sunscreen remains essential for all skin tones,” Olamiju warns.

Guzman adds that these pigmentation concerns also become especially important when we introduce aesthetic treatments such as lasers, chemical peels, or microneedling. “Certain procedures and treatment settings carry a greater risk of pigmentation changes in patients with more melanin-rich skin, so proper patient selection, device choice, and clinical expertise are critical,” Guzman notes.

Overall, smart aging should combine science, prevention, consistency, and thoughtful aesthetic care. “Aging is inevitable. How we care for ourselves throughout that process is where we have the opportunity to make a meaningful difference,” Guzman concludes.

#6627. Why Weed Might Actually Be Bad for Your Sleep

Everyone’s done it before. A pre-game gummy. A nighttime toke. Weed is, at this point, a widely used sleep aid. It usually works pretty well, too. But if you’ve made it a habit, you might just be sabotaging your shut-eye in the long run. According to a new October 2026 study, consuming pot in any form before bed causes people to have poorer quality of sleep—without them even realizing it. In other words: It has exactly the opposite of its intended effect. Here’s what you should know before popping an edible before you doze off.

The study, which was performed by Northwestern University researchers and published in JAMA Network, looked at 1,266 adults who participated in the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study, which followed participants for 35 years to determine how behavioral, biological, and environmental factors affected their risk of heart disease later in life. Of that sample size, 891 wore wrist-based activity monitors for at least a week so that researchers could examine their sleep patterns. After analyzing the data, the researchers found that those who were long-term cannabis users had “poorer objective sleep, including lower sleep efficiency, greater fragmentation, and more time awake during the night,” Dr. Thanh-Huyen Vu, an author of the study and a research associate professor of preventive medicine at Northwestern University’s Feinberg School of Medicine, tells GQ.

Here’s what all of that means: Sleep efficiency is essentially how much of the time you spend in bed you’re actually asleep. So, lower sleep efficiency means spending more time lying awake instead of sleeping while sleep fragmentation refers to how often your sleep is interrupted, like when you’re unknowingly tossing and turning to get comfortable. The researchers also looked at how much total time participants spent awake during the night. It all boils down to the fact that long-term cannabis users weren’t sleeping as soundly or as continuously throughout the night—sometimes without them even knowing it.

The researchers can’t say for certain. Because the study was observational, it only established an association between long-term cannabis exposure and poorer sleep quality.

One possibility, Vu suggests, is that cannabis may “alter normal sleep architecture,” potentially changing the way the body cycles through different sleep stages.

Over time, it’s those changes that can contribute to more nighttime awakenings, which result in less restorative sleep. She says more research is needed to understand the underlying biological mechanisms.

Deep sleep is one of the most important stages of sleep because it’s the phase when your body recovers physically, processes memory, and regulates the immune system. Interruptions in sleep result in less time during the deep sleep cycle, which inhibits your body from doing all the important things that help you function properly when you’re awake. The less deep sleep you get, the worse you feel in the morning. The reason why participants don’t pick up on these mid-sleep wake-ups is that they’re easy to forget. “Sleep trackers can capture some of these patterns, even when people don’t perceive their sleep as being particularly poor,” Vu says. It’s the same way in which you think you slept eight hours one night but woke up feeling groggy regardless.

Not necessarily. Given the sample population—middle-aged adults—the results may not apply to people in other age ranges or even those who use cannabis for medical reasons. Still, Vu says it’s important for people to understand that cannabis’s relationship with sleep may be more complicated than simply helping you drift off faster.

If you regularly use cannabis before bed, paying attention to your sleep patterns may help you better understand how it’s affecting you. Wearable sleep trackers can offer some insight into nighttime awakenings and sleep efficiency, but you won’t get the same sleep analysis if you were part of a study like this. It might be worth trying out a period where you don’t use weed to fall asleep to see if it makes a difference in whether you feel more well-rested, or your mind feels sharper. Though the study still leaves a lot of questions to be answered, its data is clear enough to make anyone with a nightly gummy habit reconsider.

#6626. Every Time Veruschka Was on the Cover of American Vogue

Veruschka, the legendary German model who helped revolutionize fashion photography during the late 1960s and early ’70s, has died at the age of 87, a family member confirmed to the German newspaper Bild.

The statuesque beauty was known for her collaborations with the leading photographers of her day—Richard Avedon, Irving Penn, and Bert Stern among them—and many of her most enduring shoots were originally published within the pages of Vogue. It was the magazine’s visionary editor in chief Diana Vreeland who famously championed the six-foot-one newcomer after discovering her in Paris and urging her to drop her aristocratic surname, recognizing her as a perfect conduit for the era’s psychedelic, boundary-pushing spirit.

As a result, she appeared on the cover of the magazine some 12 times. In the year of 1965 alone, she was a Vogue cover star on five separate occasions. Seen together, they serve as a remarkable document of fashion’s seismic shifts throughout the 1960s, her endless versatility as a model, and the remarkable alchemy she shared with many of the era’s most extraordinary image makers.

#6622. Should You Worry About That Bump on Your Chest?

If you’re like most guys, you probably have plenty of little bumps and lumps on your skin. There’s the callus on your toe from training for that 10K, the razor bumps along your neck from this morning’s shave, and the skin tag on your underarm you keep meaning to get removed. While it’s often completely fine to ignore these bumps, that isn’t always the case. Some can be a red flag worth paying attention to—especially if they’re on your chest.

While male breast cancer is rare, estimates suggest that more than 2,600 men are diagnosed with an invasive form of the disease each year in the United States, and more than 500 die, according to the American Cancer Society. And one of its telltale signs is a firm bump under or near your nipple. Below, find out more about what a breast-cancer lump may look like and four other things that could be to blame for a new bump on your chest.

There isn’t a universal description of what breast cancer lumps look like in men, but there are some common characteristics to keep in mind. “Breast cancer in men typically presents as a painless, firm, or hard lump,” says Jose Pablo Leone, MD, the director of the Program for Breast Cancer in Men at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston.

Another sign that the bump could be breast cancer is if it’s behind or very close to the nipple and areola. “Men have much less developed breast glandular tissue than women, which is why breast cancer in men most commonly develops near or behind the nipple,” says Dr. Leone. As for size even a lump as small as a pea can be cancerous, but by the time men go to the doctor, tumors are often larger than a marble, according to Dr. Leone. “In part because of the lack of awareness and screening, most men present with larger tumors,” he says. “But any size is worth mentioning to your doctor. Not all breast cancers feel the same, so any new or persistent breast lump should be evaluated by a healthcare professional.”

Your chest has a lot of oil glands, which can set the stage for pimples. “Staying in a sweaty shirt after a workout can make chest acne flare, especially if the fabric is tight and rubs against your skin,” says Elizabeth Bahar Houshmand, MD, a board-certified dermatologist based in Dallas. While blackheads and whiteheads are typically small and easy to identify, inflamed pimples or nodules may seem more alarming because they can be hard, painful, and form deep under the skin. When it comes to nodular acne specifically, you can’t treat it on your own. If that’s what you think you’re dealing with, see a dermatologist, who can prescribe an oral or topical medication to help clear it up.

“This is a collection of fat that forms under the skin,” says Sonya Kenkare, MD, a board-certified dermatologist at Illinois Dermatology Institute in Hinsdale, Illinois. “It is usually soft, not painful, and you can move it around in all different directions.” You don’t need to do anything about a lipoma, but if you want to get it removed, you can talk to a doctor about it.

When hair follicles get inflamed or infected, you can end up with folliculitis. “Folliculitis often looks like small pimples or pus-filled bumps centered around a hair follicle” says Dr. Houshmand. “They may itch or feel tender.”

Blockage or damage to a hair follicle can also cause epidermal inclusion cysts. These cysts occur when dead skin cells get trapped under the surface instead of shedding. “They feel somewhat firm and often have a central little black spot,” says Dr. Kenkare. Sometimes simply applying a warm compress to the area can help a cyst heal on its own, but a doctor can also inject it with a steroid to reduce swelling, drain it, or surgically remove it.

This condition occurs when breast tissue gets enlarged in men, and it can first appear as a lump under your nipple. “It often feels like a rubbery or firm disc beneath the nipple, and it may be tender,” says Dr. Houshmand. While gynecomastia can come on as a side effect of some medications, like antibiotics or antidepressants, or diseases like thyroid disorders, sometimes there is no clear cause at all.

If you’re starting to feel like it’s difficult to tell on your own what the lump on your chest might be, you’re not wrong. That’s why it’s best to have your primary care physician look at any new, unexplained bumps and tell you whether you need imaging, like a mammogram with an ultrasound. That may sound scary, but it’s really just covering your bases. “Uncommon things are uncommon, and breast cancer in men is uncommon,” says Dr. Leone. “You shouldn’t worry excessively about male breast cancer, but you should be aware of it.”

#6620. Veruschka: The Late ’60s Supermodel’s Best Beauty Looks of All Time

There are few faces more synonymous with the youthquake of the ’60s than Veruschka, who has sadly passed away at the age of 87.

Born Vera Gottliebe Anna Gräfin von Lehndorff-Steinort in East Prussia, the German countess was discovered at 20 years old while studying art in Florence. Soon after, she decamped to New York City, where she changed her name from Vera to Veruschka and became one of the most—if not the most—in-demand supermodels of the decade, regularly appearing in the pages of Vogue and lensed by greats such as David Bailey, Irving Penn, and Richard Avedon.

Standing six feet tall, she was a bombshell with a chiseled-by-the-gods bone structure, steely blue gaze, plush mouth, and shape-shifting champagne-blonde hair. Her “indomitable career of beauty,” as Susan Sontag once famously deemed it, was characterized by portraits of her sinewy silhouette, immortalized most notoriously in that scene from Michelangelo Antonioni’s cult 1966 film Blow-Up, where she poses for photographer David Hemmings’s camera to amorous effect.

As for her countless evocative close-ups, which showcased her otherworldly hair and makeup looks, nothing was too decorative or directional for Veruschka, and it was this perpetual gameness that made her a favorite of Diana Vreeland during her tenure at Vogue. There were her sculptural, teased-to-the-heavens, and decidedly ’60s hair looks, from a voluminous bouffant with waist-grazing lengths, to an origami-like knot, to the tornado of face-framing braids that she wore in a 1967 editorial shot by her longtime lover and collaborator Franco Rubartelli. And then there were her signature extreme lashes, which ran the gamut from classic, doll-like fringe to cast in Technicolor shades or granddaddy longlegs lengths, and were often punctuated by a sheer wash of pastel pigment on the lids, graphic winged liner, and glossy pink lips.

“The most beautiful woman in the world,” according to Avedon, and a true chameleon in every sense of the word, Veruschka’s metamorphic fluency continues to be a lethal and enduring combination in the fashion world. In fact, in 2017, Acne Studios tapped Veruschka to star in its Resort 2018 look book, where she wore the collection’s cropped jackets and slouchy trousers with a sharp slick back and statuesque swagger. Here, a look at her most striking beauty looks of all time.

#6617. How Did This 14-Year-Old Get Sam Bankman-Fried on the Phone?

Journalists who’ve been anxious about losing their jobs to artificial intelligence would be wise to focus on a different, altogether less menacing but equally impressive threat: 14-year-old Eli Goldfine, the shoestring podcaster from Westchester County who last week conducted a 90-minute interview with Sam Bankman-Fried, who’s currently serving a 25-year sentence in federal prison for orchestrating a multi-billion-dollar cryptocurrency grift.

So how, exactly, does this precocious ninth grader with braces—and not a reporter from one of the scores of legacy publications who’d surely be gunning for access to the disgraced cryptocurrency king—score an interview so coveted? “I had written about Sam on Twitter a little bit, and it got picked up by the person who was at the time running Sam’s account,” Goldfine, who hosts a podcast about prediction markets called The Supercycle, told me earlier this week. “I think they were impressed with my knowledge of various parts of his criminal case.”

Goldfine’s classmates are impressed, too, even though he’s been on the receiving end of some gentle ribbing about his on-air ad reads. But can any of them say they got Bankman-Fried to speculate on the likelihood that AI will bring about the extinction of the human race? ("Less than 50%, more than 10%," by the way). Before school’s out for Thanksgiving break, Goldfine joined GQ to talk about his media diet, dream interview subject, and the mechanics of interviewing a man behind bars.

Eli Goldfine: Wait, just to step back here. Are you printing what I'm going to say, or is this just for you to know? It's not a video on the site, right?

Okay. So my podcast is primarily about prediction markets and other broader markets. And I got into that during the 2024 election. My dad showed me Polymarket and I thought, "Wow, this is really cool. It's people staking money on different sides of an outcome. And when you put all that price signal together, it converges on a really accurate probability of a given event happening. How could I investigate this more?" So I learned more about it and I started trading on a fake-money version of Polymarket.

It's called Manifold Markets. And what's cool about that one is, anyone can create their own question rather than the platform deciding. And anyway, I got really into it and then I was like, “I'll write a couple articles about this because I have some ideas.” And then I started doing interviews and it all kind of came out from that.

I think sports betting, like FanDuel and DraftKings—this stuff obviously serves very little utility because it's just the company offering these bets to the gamblers and there's no really accurate price signal coming out of that. So does that serve such an important function? Probably not. And it's fair to say the same about prediction markets on sports. Does anyone really need to know the outcome of a sports game that badly? I mean, probably not. I don't have anything against it per se, because people spend money for entertainment on other things. I mean, this is another way to spend your money. But it's not as valuable as prediction markets in some other categories. Right?

I mean, I think I've just always had a motivation to learn more about what I'm interested in. So when I start learning about something, I just get it all in my head and then I can talk about it pretty competently, I guess. I wouldn't consider myself to have natural interviewing skill. I just think I know a lot about the things that I'm interested in.

So for news, mostly Bloomberg. For social media, mostly Twitter. And then I also read articles on Substack.

So I think I had written about Sam on Twitter a little bit, and it got picked up by the person who was at the time running Sam's Twitter account. And they said, "I run this Twitter account now, but I think you have some smart ideas about Sam. Would you be interested in taking over the Twitter account?" And I was like, "Oh, yeah, that could be fun." And my dad was like, "No, you can't do that. I don't want to get sued or anything." So we ended up talking to Sam's parents about it, and they were disappointed that I wouldn't be able to take over the Twitter account. But as an alternative, they proposed, "You should just interview Sam for your podcast." So I just thought, "Wow, that's a great idea. Let's do that."

Oh, I don't know. I think they were impressed with my knowledge of various parts of his criminal case, which we actually didn't cover very much during our podcast together, since it's already been widely covered. But, yeah, I think I just had learned a lot about the case and they were like, "Well, maybe we want someone who knows a lot about the case to be able to take over his Twitter."

I don't know. I might want to skip that one for legal reasons.

I mean, I've watched so many of his other interviews, both when he was behind bars and before that, and I feel like he talks the same way to everyone. So I'm 14, you would expect maybe the average person is going to talk a little bit differently to a 14-year-old interviewer. But for him, I think it was pretty much the same, which is kind of what I expected. He's very consistent when he's talking to different people.

So when he picked up and was like, "Hi, it's Sam," I was like, "Wow, I've heard him say this in so many other interviews, but he's talking to me. That's crazy." He also called 15 minutes before the scheduled time, so I was panicking a little bit trying to get all my questions in order and deciding what order I was going to ask them in. I mean, it was pretty intense. And also, it was split up over two days in three hour windows during each day, since he can only call for 15 minutes at a time. So that was a little bit stressful.

I mean, it's mostly what I expected. He just hadn't really gone on the record about it specifically, which is why I wanted to ask him. I think his views are pretty common. He's a part of the effective altruism community. So I wasn't so surprised when he said he thought there was a 25% chance of AI destroying humanity. Obviously, if it's the average person, that might seem a little surprising. But knowing him, I wasn't very surprised.

I think there's going to be a lot of benefit in the short term, especially when we're seeing the rate of technological progress. Just in the past few months, AI has solved multiple millennium problems, which has been a huge deal. So I think there's definitely potential of AI curing diseases over the short term. But in the long term, you have to consider that there's a few examples of less intelligent things controlling more intelligent things, and that's kind of the whole point that the doomers are trying to make. Just that, when humans were smarter than the next smartest animal, we’re the ones who dominated, right?

At the end of the interview, I asked him what I call the coin flip question. "Would you take a 51-49 bet of doubling the world or destroying it?" Yeah. I mean, there's something funny that happened. Someone at my school walked up to me and they were like, "Hey, are you the kid who ..." Actually, wait. I actually don't want to go there.

But they were all excited. They thought it was pretty funny, and then they were impressed that it got as many views as it did. So that's been the less good side of things.

Ninth grade. And I live in Westchester County, New York.

#6613. Emma Corrin’s Subversive Suiting Game Is Like No Other

By now, it’s well-documented that Emma Corrin is a true red carpet star. The actor and their right-hand stylist Harry Lambert are a true match made in heaven. Together, they always find looks that are forward-thinking, intriguing, and slightly unconventional. (Remember Corrin’s pantless Miu Miu look at the Venice Film Festival, for one?)

This month, Corrin is continuing that energy throughout the Pride and Prejudice press tour. The Netflix miniseries reboot sees Corrin portray Elizabeth Bennet, premiering December 3. For their latest fashion serve-upon-serve, Corrin has been focusing in on the classic suit, finding fresh ways to twist and subvert it. Over the course of the past month, the star has stepped out in a few different takes on the tailored two-piece, each time finding a new detail or beat.

Things kicked off at a Pride and Prejudice fan Q&A event at the British Library earlier this month. Corrin emerged wearing a Chanel suit from Matthieu Blazy’s spring 2027 collection. The tailored checkered jacket and trouser felt fresh, thanks to the whimsical details like the playing card-themed buttons including squared heart, spade, clover, and diamond decals.

For an appearance at the Heart Breakfast Radio Studios yesterday, Corrin followed up the kitschy suit with another win—this time, by British designer Talia Byre, from her spring 2027 collection. The slightly shrunken, high-buttoned blazer felt very reminiscent of the ’90s, when the cuts were slim and the minimalist black suit reigned supreme. Three decades later, the look still feels modern.

And just today, Corrin broke away from the timeless suit but kept things streamlined in a long, sharp-shouldered black overcoat and white flared jeans. The peek of a studded belt? The hint of a fierce pointed pump? Chef’s kiss. Corrin’s approach to the dressy and professional is proof that you can suit up without looking like a total corporate drone. If Emma Corrin worked in a fluorescent-lit cubicle, they’d definitely be the coolest person in the office.

#6607. Can Your Home Boost Your Endorphins? 7 Simple Tips for a Healthier, Happier Living Space

On a recent cold Sunday morning, I had no interest in doing anything except hiding from the world. Then I did a few small tasks that completely shifted my mood. First, I spritzed a home fragrance with notes of orange and cinnamon around my apartment; next, I raised the blinds to let in some sunlight and tidied up the living room—clearing away clutter, folding blankets, and fluffing the pillows on the couch. As I did, I recalled the words of Loewe’s perfumer, Nuria Cruelles, about one of her candles: “It has the power to transform your house into a home.” That’s exactly what I was doing, simply by adding a bit of scent and straightening up. Another expert, Dr. Rodrigo Arteaga, explains that anyone can turn their home into a “place that improves their health” by following a few simple habits.

There are indeed many small routines we can adopt to turn our home—the place where we relax and let our guard down—into an environment that fosters well-being. Psychologist María Martínez echoes this, encouraging people to practice the Japanese philosophy of kaizen, which emphasizes the transformative power of making gradual, continuous improvements to our lives. “It’s important to create an environment where you look around and like what you see,” she says. “This releases endorphins and makes you feel good. If instead, everywhere you look, there’s a reminder of a task you need to do, something unattractive, or clutter that causes stress, you’ll end up feeling worse. If it gets bad enough, you’ll soon stop wanting to be in your own home. You’ll find reasons to leave or stay late at the office, coming home only to sleep. These are all signs that you need to make changes—not just in your life, but in your home, which should serve as a sanctuary where you can recharge.”

Here are seven practical tips to help create a home environment that helps boost your mental and physical health.

When Florence Pugh was asked in a recent Vogue interview what a perfect day off looks like for her, one of the first things she mentioned was buying flowers. “I love going to my florist and putting together a beautiful bouquet; it makes me so happy,” she said. She’s not alone. According to a study by Dr. Nancy Etcoff of Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, flowers ward off worry, anxiety, and sadness. Study participants felt noticeably better after having flowers in their homes for just a few days—and tended to place them in the kitchen, dining room, and living room, the spaces where they spent most of their time.

Whenever possible, open your curtains and blinds in the morning. As Dr. Arteaga points out, “This gives your brain a powerful signal to synchronize its biological clock. Natural light helps your body recognize when it’s day and when it’s night, giving you more energy during the daytime and helping you rest better at night.” After dusk, create “light islands” inspired by the Danish philosophy of hygge, which offers plenty of ideas for designing a wellness-focused home. As Meik Wiking explains in his book My Hygge Home, you can bring warmth to dark corners of a living room using lamps that cast light downward and bulbs that emit a soft, warm glow. Floor or table lamps placed near a sofa or reading chair work especially well. For more general lighting in spaces meant for relaxation, hygge experts recommend ceiling or wall fixtures with glass or fabric shades that diffuse light gently, rather than harsh overhead chandeliers or pendants.

Studies show that listening to music you love provides an immediate boost to your well-being. “Music has an instant, almost magical effect on us,” explains psychologist Marta Calderero. “Within just a few seconds of hearing a favorite song, your brain is flooded with endorphins and oxytocin. That’s why you suddenly feel that rush of euphoria and such an intimate connection to a track. And it doesn’t stop there—after a couple of minutes, the brain begins releasing dopamine, making us enjoy each second a little more than the last. It’s the most beautiful way I know to regulate emotions and reconnect with the present moment.”

Hygge inspired another recommendation on our list. As Wiking explains, styling a small corner of your home with cozy lighting, blankets (a hygge staple), pillows, a plush rug, and a few favorite objects creates a dedicated spot to unplug from the world. It’s a simple way to build an inviting nook that signals to your brain that you’re in a safe space where it’s okay to relax and unwind.

Going barefoot indoors is another of Dr. Arteaga’s recommendations, and Beatriz Crespo, an expert in healthy micro-habits, seconds the idea. Beyond its physical perks—like improved circulation and balance—walking barefoot reduces stress and encourages relaxation through direct contact between the ground and the nerve-rich soles of your feet.

Proper ventilation offers clear microbiological benefits, as biologist María Dolores Cima Cabal explains: “It helps reduce the density of microorganisms that accumulate inside the home.” At the same time, it delivers real psychological perks, since breathing fresh air reenergizes the body and supplies oxygen to the brain. A Harvard University study confirms that cognitive function can suffer—and reaction times slow down—in stuffy environments.

Returning to that chilly Sunday morning at the start of this piece, candles have a unique ability to turn a house into a home through the evocative power of scent. When you choose an appealing fragrance—whether as a room spray or a candle—your brain registers it as a cue that you’re somewhere you can let your guard down. “Smell is the sense that most powerfully triggers memories, and the one our brain responds to with the greatest intensity,” concludes Calderero. “It forms a direct link between a scent and an emotion. If you keep a signature scent at home, that olfactory connection becomes so strong that the moment you smell it, your brain associates it with rest, comfort, and warmth. Choosing a specific fragrance helps your brain recognize that it’s in a space where it doesn’t need to stay on high alert—and your nervous system naturally slows down.”

#6606. GQ’s Best Gifts for Men 2026: 70+ Editor-Approved Presents

There's no shortage of stuff to buy for men. Stuff worth giving? That's another story. Fortunately, finding stuff worth giving is a salaried position around here. The results of that extensive retail research are all here: a carefully considered mix of great clothes, clever gadgets, handsome home goods, and a few things he probably wouldn't think to buy himself. We keep this guide updated throughout the year, so below you'll find our latest favorites alongside a few perennial heaters, all handpicked to make your gift-giving duties a little easier.

Still got names to cross off your list? Browse the rest of our gift guides and sign up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for a steady supply of good ideas.

This Banana Republic glen plaid double-breasted jacket features a rarely seen 2x1 button stance, which makes it a touch more casual but no less handsome.

Among Ralph Lauren's many contributions to American fashion is transforming the denim shirt from a Western novelty into a staple of the modern wardrobe. This weathered slub denim version is a handsome example, and something he'll wear for years to come.

Few knits occupy a place in the menswear pantheon quite like J.Crew's rollneck sweater. With its relaxed weave and raglan sleeves, it's an enduring heater that makes for an easy gift.

What makes Morjas' Belgian loafer so irresistible to those who've had the good fortune to wear it is just how comfortable it is. Doesn't hurt that it's also clean, understated, and versatile as all get-out.

Maple's Orbit bracelet is a great little way to add a fleck of personality to an otherwise understated fit. And if this design is a little too out-there for his taste, you may have to look elsewhere entirely. That's kind of Maple's whole thing.

Smaller, thinner cases are great, and the Timex Marlin is a stone-cold minimalist classic in that world. But it also sells out, so allow us to recommend another, newer Timex gem: the Marlin Jet Titanium. He'll love that it's an automatic, too.

Patagonia's Snap-T is an icon, and this new Re-Tool Air version gives it a fresh spin with an exclusive Polartec fleece that's remarkably lightweight, wonderfully warm, and made from 100% recycled polyester.

This merino wool crewneck from Arc'teryx is lightweight, great at regulating temperature, and just as good worn on its own as it is layered under a sweater or jacket. A go-to layering piece for just about any wardrobe.

If you ask us, the Moon Shoe is one of the Swoosh's best releases of the year. A perfectly retro, low-profile runner with a refreshingly affordable price tag.

A great hoodie is essential, and Reigning Champ nails fit-meets-function better than most, with an aesthetic inspired by old-school athletic training gear. This one is cut from the brand’s signature midweight terry, which is soft and substantial without feeling bulky.

A man can never have enough flannels. Filson's Rangeland is made from brushed 5.5-ounce cotton, and we're partial to the red and gray plaid.

Massachusetts-based Steele Canvas has been making sturdy canvas goods for generations, and its Everyday Tote is exactly the sort of gift they'll most definitely get some use out of.

When we think of field watches, we think of Hamilton. This no-nonsense mechanical number is hard to beat in the category, and you could spend a lot more on a lot less.

A good pair of cowboy boots can do wonders for a fit, and Tecovas' Warren makes a strong case for adding a little yee-haw to the rotation. With classic flame stitching and a sharp cutter toe, they're more versatile than you might think.

3sixteen's asymmetrical fleece is freaky, but not too freaky, with a wide boatneck, an off-center zipper at the neck, and an oversized pocket with a zip closure. There's a lot going on, but the proportions are spot-on.

Some of the best stuff Miansai makes is low-key its bead and stone jewelry. The Avi necklace is a welcome change of pace from the usual gold and silver.

John Smedley has been making knitwear in England for more than 200 years, and there's a reason it's still considered some of the best in the biz. This wool polo might look simple, but the quality of the knit, the fit, and the finishing make it something special.

OrSlow's 105 jeans have a classic straight leg and medium rise, with the kind of easy, timeless fit that never goes out of style. A very good upgrade for anyone whose denim rotation could use a little love.

Yes, it costs a pretty penny. But it also might be one of the coolest scarves we’ve ever seen: so robust you can wrap it around yourself a few times like a sweater, at which point the price starts to make more sense. Oh, and it’s Burberry.

Movado's iconic Museum Watch has been a masterclass in minimalism since 1947, with a Bauhaus-inspired dial that's blank save for a single dot at 12 o'clock. A remarkably sleek timepiece, especially at this price.

Some days call for a full wallet, others for just the essentials. Coach's 3-in-1 gives him both, with a removable ID insert that works just as well on its own when he wants to travel a little lighter.

For the record, we're all for giving socks as presents, provided they're of the same caliber as those from Japan's Rototo.

Quince is one of our first stops for affordable cashmere, but its merino wool offerings ain't too shabby either. Take this sweater, which it done up in cable-knit for a little somethin' somethin'.

Blundstone introduced its Heritage boot this year, a decidedly more upscale take on the brand's beloved Chelsea. Handmade from premium leather, it's also finished with a Goodyear welt that allows it to be resoled for years to come.

Come for the three iconic Byredo scents, which you can spritz according to whatever the mood calls for. Stay for the handsome leather case, which is almost reason enough to gift the set on its own.

Plenty of dopp kits come in sleek leather (no shade), and plenty of designer versions cost a small fortune (some shade). But most guys just want something that looks good and can take a beating on the road. Filson knows how to do that.

Bar soaps have officially entered the elevated grooming arena, with better ingredients and better scents. Made in France, this bar adds a pop of color by the tub, lathers like a dream, and carries Frama's gorgeous Herbarium aroma that lingers on skin long after the shower.

Bleu de Chanel's Parfum takes everything great about the original and turns it up a notch. Still zesty and botanical, but with sandalwood and tonka bean lending a richer, smoother finish.

Released this year, Braun's Nevo is arguably the best and most advanced foil shaver on the market today, and our own testing backs that up. Given the price tag, it's exactly the sort of splurge that makes for a great gift.

Vitamins B and C do wonders for the skin, and Aesop's B Triple C Facial Balancing Gel is packed with both. Deeply hydrating yet leaving a matte finish, it was a game changer when it debuted over 20 years ago, and it's still elite after all these years.

If he’s taking skincare cues from anyone, it should be Pharrell, who apparently doesn’t age. The multihyphenate’s skincare brand, Humanrace, has a Rejuvenating Face Mask featuring a peptide trio complex to keep your lucky guy looking chipper.

The Philips OneBlade 360 is a little groomer we love for its versatility. There’s really nothing quite like it out there, and it can handle just about any hairy situation.

Dior seems to drop a new olfactory banger every few months, and Bois d'Argent is one of the latest. Smooth woods, amber, and rich iris mingle with frankincense for a scent that's warm, elegant, and easy to wear just about anywhere.

Wonder Valley's newish Wild Garden hand wash puts olive oil to good use, whipping up a rich, softening lather with a cedar-and-herb scent that brings a little of the great outdoors to the sink.

A moisturizer is a no-brainer, but a serum signals one is getting extra serious about skincare. Caldera + Lab makes that addition easy: a few pumps deliver vitamin C, collagen amino acids, and skin-soothing botanicals to brighten, firm, and soften fine lines.

We've been longtime fans of Dr. Dennis Gross's Alpha Beta Universal Daily Peel pads, which make good skincare almost embarrassingly easy. A couple of swipes help exfoliate dead skin, smooth texture, and brighten the complexion.

Tower 28's travel-size SOS set packs everything they need to stay fresh on the go. A little skincare insurance for wherever the holidays take them.

Salt & Stone makes one of our favorite body washes, and this mini set lets them take the whole lineup for a spin.

With these hydrating eye patches from one of the best grooming brands to do it, no one will ever know he didn't get his proper eight hours last night.

You can buy all the fancy sunscreen you want, but convenience decides if you actually wear it. Freaks of Nature’s SPF 50 stick—small, glide-on, reef safe, and water-resistant for 80 minutes—nails it.

The LED mask market is booming, and Omnilux is at the top of the heap. This one is specifically designed and FDA-cleared for men’s typically thicker facial skin, targeting fine lines, firmness, and overall health, while helping calm any redness from shaving. In other words, it’s a Michael Myers-like mask that promises scary-good skin with consistency and patience.

#6602. Who Is Malin Akerman’s Husband, Jack Donnelly?

The Hunting Wives star married the British actor in 2018

Malin Akerman may stir up romantic trouble as Margo Banks, the notorious ringleader of The Hunting Wives, but off screen, her love life is much less chaotic. The actress has been happily married to fellow actor Jack Donnelly since 2018, and over the years, the two have even found ways to merge their professional and personal lives.

Akerman and Donnelly have collaborated on several projects, including four movies (and an NSFW sex scene, but more on that below). In a 2023 interview with People, the actress opened up about their relationship, crediting her husband with helping her become a better communicator.

“He’s allowed me to be vulnerable and lean into him a bit, and it’s been beautiful to be able to communicate with someone who’s your partner,” she said of their marriage.

Ahead, everything you need to know about Jack Donnelly, his career, and his marriage with Akerman.

Donnelly was born in Bournemouth, England, on October 28, 1985, and later attended the Central School of Speech and Drama in London. He made his acting debut in 2011 on the Nickelodeon series House of Anubis. Two years later, he landed a breakout lead role in the BBC’s series Atlantis, as Jason—which remains one of his best-known roles to date.

In addition to acting, Donnelly has branched out behind the camera as a television writer and director. He wrote, directed, and starred in the short comedy series The Players, which debuted in 2023.

The couple’s love story began with a family connection. Donnelly first met Akerman through her younger sister, whose boyfriend was friends with him at drama school. During a 2018 appearance on Live With Kelly and Ryan, the actress explained that she had actually known Donnelly for several years before their relationship turned romantic.

“I had known him for the past four years but didn’t see him,” she recalled. “Then all of a sudden he came back from England like a year-and-a-half ago, and I went, ‘Wow, have you always been this cute?’”

Akerman announced the couple’s engagement via Instagram in October 2017. Sharing a selfie with Donnelly and flashing her new engagement ring, she captioned the post, “This sweet and loving man has stepped into our lives and stole both our hearts,” she wrote, referring to her and her son. “I think we’re gonna keep him around for a while,” she continued with a wink.

Akerman and Donnelly tied the knot a little over a year later, on December 1, 2018, in a beach ceremony held in Tulum, Mexico. “It was all about being authentic...not adhering to somebody else’s standard of what a wedding should be,” Akerman told Brides.

“We wanted something beautiful and lush,” she continued, sharing more about their wedding venue. “When we visited Papaya Playa Project [in Tulum], we fell in love with the boho vibes and beach setting.”

In 2023, Akerman shared new photos from the beachside wedding on Instagram to celebrate their five-year anniversary.

When discussing her engagement on Live With Kelly and Ryan in 2018, Akerman also shared how excited her son, Sebastian, was about the news. The actress shares Sebastian with her ex-husband, musician Roberto Zincone, and recalled his excited reaction when she told him that she and Donnelly were getting married. “He jumped up on the couch and went, ‘Yay, we’re getting married!’” she said.

In another 2018 interview with Us Weekly, Akerman gushed about the close bond Donnelly had already formed with her then-five-year-old son. “They’re inseparable,” she said. “It makes my heart warm. I’m very glad to be bringing Jack into our lives for good.”

Over the years, the three have also made several red-carpet appearances together, offering a glimpse into their life as a family.

Akerman and Donnelly have shared the screen in four films so far: Friendsgiving, A Week in Paradise, Slayers, and Us or Them. Their first movie together was the 2020 comedy Friendsgiving, in which they played a couple—and even had to film a steamy sex scene. During a 2020 appearance on The Talk, Akerman opened up about filming the “crazy S&M scene.”

“[It was] just like being in our home,” she joked when asked what it was like filming the sex scene. She added that she was glad to have her husband as her costar. “Any chance I get to have him do a scene like that, who better than to do it with than your husband?” she said. “It’s a really, kind of, intimate, crazy scene, and thank God we know each other well enough instead of just meeting somebody on the first day and [doing] this crazy S&M scene. It was lovely to have him there.”

During a November 2026 appearance on The Drew Barrymore Show, Akerman and her The Hunting Wives costar Brittany Snow discussed Snow’s recent engagement to fiancé Hunter Moreno. When Barrymore asked if their significant others got along too, Akerman gushed, “They’re so close!”

“We call them all the Hunting Husbands,” Akerman added, sharing their nickname for all the boyfriends and husbands of the cast.
