Researchers have zeroed in on a genetic variant in the human brain that came from Neanderthals, and it might protect us from schizophrenia.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A newfound genetic variant inherited from Neanderthals may shrink a part of modern-human brains without having any meaningful effects on mental ability, and it might also reduce the risk of schizophrenia, a new study finds.

"Genetic differences between Neanderthals and modern humans still influence our brains today," study co-author Hugo Zeberg, an evolutionary geneticist at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Germany, told Live Science. Zeberg and his colleague Svante Pääbo detailed their findings Nov. 16 in the journal PNAS.

Before they went extinct around 40,000 years ago, Neanderthals were among the closest relatives of modern humans. More than a decade of research has shown that Neanderthals and modern humans once interbred. Most people not of sub-Saharan ancestry living today possess about 2% Neanderthal ancestry.

Neanderthals' skulls were larger and more elongated than modern humans'. One reason for the differences has to do with the occipital lobe, the smallest of the brain's four lobes, which sits in the back of the skull. The occipital lobe houses the visual cortex, which helps process signals from the eyes. This area was relatively larger in Neanderthals than it is in modern humans.

In the new study, the researchers analyzed modern-human genomes for genetic variants that are related to occipital lobe size and were also likely inherited from Neanderthals. They discovered one such variant associated with the DAAM1 gene, which a 2019 study linked with brain development. This genetic variant was found only in modern humans outside Africa and was seen in five Neanderthal genomes.

Curiously, the Neanderthal variant the scientists detected in modern-human genomes led to an approximately 0.05-cubic-inch (0.85 cubic centimeters) reduction in occipital lobe size per copy of the variant in an individual. This means that the Neanderthal gene was linked to a slightly smaller brain size in modern humans.

A Neanderthal variant can have a relatively strong effect on brain anatomy without affecting intelligence, while also reducing schizophrenia risk.

This effect is the opposite of what experts expected based on Neanderthals' large skull size, Tony Capra, an evolutionary geneticist at the University of California, San Francisco, who was not involved in the research, told Live Science.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

However, it's important to remember that this one gene variant "does not reflect the full set of variations that might have been present in Neanderthals that might have affected the shape and size of their brain structures," Capra noted.

Zeberg and Pääbo also discovered that having two copies of the DAAM1 gene variant was associated with a nearly 10% reduction in the chances of having schizophrenia in modern humans. But there was no apparent link between the variant and intelligence in modern humans.

"A Neanderthal variant can have a relatively strong effect on brain anatomy without affecting intelligence, while also reducing schizophrenia risk," Zeberg said.

Symptoms of schizophrenia can include altered perceptions of reality, such as visual hallucinations and problems with processing visual signals. This makes it "tempting to speculate" that this Neanderthal gene variant's effects on schizophrenia might be associated with the visual cortex. However, there is currently no evidence for such a link, Zeberg said.

Future research along these lines could analyze how other Neanderthal genetic variants influenced modern humans, Capra said, "to see if they had a consistent effect on us." Looking into Neanderthal variants that are missing from modern-human genomes could "show us what makes us modern humans as opposed to them," Capra added.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Zeberg, H., & Pääbo, S. (2026). A Neandertal-derived genetic variant reduces occipital brain volume in present-day humans. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 123(48). https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2624837123

#6502. Butter Mochi Cake With Maple-Miso Pecans

For Shuai Wang, chef of King BBQ in North Charleston, South Carolina, mochi brings back memories of holidays with family. His other dessert love? Classic Southern pecan pie. This Hawaiian-style butter mochi cake draws on both, pairing a rich, chewy cake with a generous layer of maple-miso pecans.

The batter gets its signature bounce from mochiko, a distinct style of rice flour that gives butter mochi its chewy texture—not the fluffy crumb of a conventional cake. Coconut milk and melted butter add richness, while the pecans provide crunch. Let the cake cool completely before slicing so the texture has time to set.

The secret to the pecan topping is a little white or yellow miso, which brings savory depth to the maple syrup, much like the salt in salted caramel. The nuts need only a brief head start in the oven; they’ll continue to toast as the cake bakes.

Can I use regular rice flour instead of mochiko?

No. Mochiko, also called sweet or glutinous rice flour, has a different starch composition from regular rice flour. It’s responsible for butter mochi’s characteristic springy, slightly sticky chew. Regular rice flour or all-purpose flour won’t produce the same texture.

White and yellow miso are both good choices for this cake. White miso tends to be milder and slightly sweeter, while yellow miso has a somewhat more pronounced savory flavor. Either adds complexity to the maple-coated pecans without overwhelming their buttery, nutty flavor. Learn more about the different types of miso and how to use them.

Mochiko is naturally gluten-free, despite the sometimes confusing name glutinous rice flour. This recipe can be gluten-free, but check your miso: Some varieties contain barley or wheat. If you’re baking for someone who needs to avoid gluten, choose a miso labeled gluten-free and check your other packaged ingredients.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lightly oil a rimmed baking sheet with vegetable oil. Whisk 2 Tbsp. pure maple syrup and 2 tsp. white or yellow miso (gluten-free if needed) in a medium bowl until smooth. Add 8 oz. raw pecans, coarsely chopped (about 2 cups) and 1 Tbsp. sugar and toss until evenly coated. Spread out on prepared baking sheet; bake until fragrant and matte looking, 6–8 minutes (nuts won’t be fully toasted). Let cool.

Lightly grease a 9"-diameter cake pan with unsalted butter and line bottom with a parchment paper round. Vigorously whisk 2 large eggs, 1¼ cups (250 g) sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth. Add one 13.5-oz. can unsweetened coconut milk, well shaken, heated slightly if fat is solid, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, and whisk well. Add 1⅔ cups (254 g) mochiko and 1 tsp. baking powder; whisk vigorously until combined and batter is smooth and thick. Scrape batter into prepared pan.

Toss pecans to break up any clumps and scatter evenly over batter, going all the way to the edges (it may seem like a lot). Bake cake until sides start to pull away from pan, top is golden brown, and a tester inserted into the center comes out clean (some pecans will sink), 50–55 minutes. If pecans begin to brown too quickly, loosely tent pan with foil. Transfer to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan 15 minutes. Turn cake out onto rack; peel away parchment and discard. Carefully turn cake right side up and let cool completely (at least 1 hour).

To serve, slice cake and top with scoops of vanilla ice cream.

Do Ahead: Cake can be made 1 day ahead. Store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

Editor’s note: This recipe was first published in our August 2023 issue and has been updated with additional guidance. Head this way for more of our favorite pecan recipes →

#6500. Japanese Sweet Potato Chaat

Every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

To a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz. [170 g]), leaves and stems, 1 bunch mint (about 2 oz. [55 g]), leaves and tender stems, 6 green Thai chiles or 2 serranos, stemmed (more if you want it spicier), ½ cup (120 ml) lime juice (from about 5 limes), 2 tsp. cumin seeds, 1½ tsp. fine sea salt, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. chaat masala. Pulse for a few seconds in intervals until the ingredients are pulverized into a smooth paste. Transfer to an airtight container and store until ready to use, up to 1 week in the refrigerator or 1 month in the freezer.

Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

Drizzle the sheet with extra-virgin olive oil and place 1½ lb. (680 g) Japanese or Korean sweet potatoes, ends trimmed, halved lengthwise, cut-side down. Bake for 60 to 70 minutes, until golden and caramelized on the cut side and cooked through and tender; a knife inserted into the center of the potato should slide through easily. Let rest for 5 to 8 minutes. Once cool enough to handle, cut the sweet potatoes into 1" to 2" [2.5 to 5 cm] pieces.

To a small bowl, add ½ cup (120 g) plain whole-milk yogurt or sour cream and ½ tsp. fine sea salt and whisk to combine. If you’re using sour cream, thin it out with a little water.

Place the sweet potatoes on a serving platter and drizzle the yogurt, ½ cup Evergreen Chutney, 3 Tbsp. tamarind concentrate or paste, and 2 Tbsp. lime juice evenly all over. Sprinkle with 1 medium red tomato (5 oz. [140 g]), finely chopped, 1 small red onion (7 oz. [200 g]), finely chopped, 2 Tbsp. chopped cilantro leaves and tender stems, 1 tsp. chaat masala, 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, thinly sliced, and crispy sev and serve immediately.

Do Ahead: You can make the individual components a day ahead of time and store them in airtight containers in the refrigerator, then assemble to serve.

On Wednesday (Nov. 18), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft became the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth. Here, we look back at its most important discoveries, seen through groundbreaking space photos.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Early Wednesday (Nov. 18), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hit a new space exploration milestone: The probe, which launched in 1977, became the first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth.

The milestone is largely symbolic, but it comes with practical consequences: While Voyager 1 cruises through interstellar space at roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from our planet, it now takes a full 24 hours for radio signals moving at the speed of light to get from Voyager 1 to Earth, and vice versa.

The growing space between Voyager and Earth makes it increasingly hard to troubleshoot problems on the nearly 50-year-old probe. But with Voyager 1 still collecting data with two of its science instruments, which are expected to stay powered up into the 2030s, NASA scientists say one thing is certain: The spacecraft isn't done surprising us.

"What Voyager has taught me is to expect the unexpected," Linda Spilker, who joined the Voyager team in 1977 and is the mission's current project scientist, told Live Science in an interview. "So many times the ideas and theories we had, Voyager was able to prove them wrong."

Here, we look back at some of Voyager 1's most groundbreaking discoveries, told through its incredible photos.

NASA's Voyager 1 probe launches atop a Titan/Centaur-6 launch vehicle from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

NASA's Voyager 2 probe launched before Voyager 1, on Aug. 20, 1977. Voyager 1 took off a few weeks later, on Sept. 5. (The two spacecraft took slightly different routes through the solar system, allowing Voyager 1 to reach interstellar space first after a gravity boost from Jupiter and Saturn.)

Spilker, who joined NASA right out of college, attended the historic Voyager 2 launch and recalls "that feeling of watching the rocket lift up off the launchpad, feeling the roar of those rocket engines and knowing this was a mission going to visit places I'd always been curious about."

A few weeks after launching, Voyager 1 took this photo of a crescent Earth and moon from 7.25 million miles (11.66 million km) from Earth.

On its way to the outer solar system, Voyager 1 snapped this image of a crescent Earth and its moon, captured in the same frame for the first time ever.

Voyager 1 photographed Jupiter from January to April 1979, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As the spacecraft zoomed closer to the giant planet, it snapped an image every 96 seconds, creating this incredible time-lapse animation of the planet's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of one Earth month

The close-up view showed that Jupiter is a far more dynamic world than previously thought. But Voyager also made key discoveries about the planet's many moons.

While passing by the Jovian moon Io, Voyager 1 witnessed an explosion: the first volcanic eruption ever seen beyond Earth. This proved that there were other geologically active worlds in our solar system, opening up entirely new avenues of inquiry and exploration.

A blue eruption on Jupiter's moon Io, the first volcanic eruption seen on another world

"Going in, we thought that the moons would look a lot like our own moon: ancient dead worlds," Spilker said. "And yet we found out they were very different worlds — like Io with active volcanoes. It was just an incredible change in our thinking."

By viewing these eruptions, scientists saw parts of Io's surface being changed in real time. "As we got closer [to Io], scientists kept saying the surface is getting younger and younger, because they didn't see any big craters, no medium sized craters, no little craters — until finally parts of its surface are just minutes old," Spilker said.

A mosaic view of Callisto taken from Voyager 1 photos at a distance of about 250,000 miles (400,000 km)

Some of Voyager's close-up observations also confirmed old theories. For example, Voyager 1's flyby of the moon Callisto in March 1979 revealed vast fields of well-preserved impact craters, proving that Callisto was geologically dead.

Jupiter and its thin ring of dust backlit by the sun in a Voyager 1 image

A final surprise at Jupiter came when Voyager 1 swooped around the planet's nightside, seeing the gas giant backlit by the sun. This view revealed a thin ring system around the planet, made partly of the dust particles Io spewed into space.

Voyager 1 reached Saturn in November 1980 and made its closest approach to the planet on Nov. 12 of that year. Four days later, the spacecraft took this image of the planet's nightside, showing a broad shadow cast onto the surrounding rings.

"That is one of my favorite pictures: an outbound image, taken by Voyager looking at [Saturn] in a way you could never see from the Earth," Spilker said, noting that we can only ever see Saturn's sunlit side from our planet. "The rings just look so beautiful shining there, and you can actually see the shadow of Saturn on the rings themselves. It's a really, really special picture."

In addition to discovering a previously unknown ring, Voyager 1 spotted five new moons around Saturn and took close-up photos of several other known satellites.

Voyager 1's closeup view of Titan revealed a dense, hazy atmosphere

The mission required Voyager to swing by the moon Titan in order to bend the probe's trajectory, sending it away from the solar system's planetary plane and toward a rendezvous with interstellar space. Before that, Voyager 1 revealed Titan's atmosphere to be so hazy that it completely obscured the moon's surface. This showed that Titan's clogged atmosphere was far denser than those of Earth and Mars.

By 1990, Voyager 1 was so far from the planetary plane that our solar system's planets looked like little more than specks of light. But before turning off its camera for good, Voyager 1 looked back at our cosmic neighborhood and took some of the most iconic space photos of all time.

In a series of 64 images taken from roughly 40 times Earth's distance from the sun, Voyager snapped its solar system "family portrait," a mosaic of images capturing six planets together for the first time. The portrait included views of Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Frames from Voyager 1's family portrait showing Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.

The image of Earth from this collection is famously known as the "Pale Blue Dot."

"We took the pictures of the planets in color, and that one is especially one of my favorites," Spilker said. "There's Earth captured in a sunbeam. A tiny world less than a pixel in size representing all the life that we know in our solar system — just a very special image reminding us just how special and precious our planet is."

Earth appears as a pale blue dot in this iconic Voyager 1 image

Voyager 1 turned off its camera immediately after taking these images, concluding its role as the greatest tourist in the history of our solar system. In 2012, Voyager 1 passed beyond the heliopause — the boundary where the sun's radiation gives way to the interstellar medium — becoming the first interstellar spacecraft in history.

Voyager 2 crossed the same boundary in 2018 and is expected to reach its own light-day in 2035. In the meantime, several science instruments remain active on both probes, allowing them to measure the strange and mysterious environment between stars.

Even way out there, the probes are still detecting whispers of the sun's power.

"We are still seeing effects from the sun that come out, hit the heliopause, and send shocks and pressure fronts out into the interstellar medium," Spilker said. "I wonder where we will finally reach the point where the sun doesn't influence what we're seeing, and we're in the pristine interstellar medium — and I hope that happens while Voyager 1 is still operating."

#6495. Failproof Homestyle Chicken Kari

This recipe is inspired by the garam masala my mother used to make back in India. Just a pinch adds incredible depth and flavor to both meat and vegetable dishes—it’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional. And now you can use it too! This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again. If you prefer a sweeter blend, add more cinnamon and fennel seeds; if you want a spicier kick, increase the black pepper and cloves.

In a small bowl, toss 12 dried bay leaves, 12 whole cloves, 5 black cardamom pods, 4 whole star anise pods, three 3" (7.5-cm) cinnamon sticks, 1 whole nutmeg, 3 Tbsp. coriander seeds, 3 Tbsp. whole mace fronds, 2 Tbsp. cumin seeds, 1 Tbsp. black peppercorns, and 2 tsp. white poppy seeds to combine.

Heat a medium dry skillet over low heat until hot. Add the spice mixture and toast until slightly fragrant, about 45 seconds. Transfer back to the bowl and let cool.

Transfer the whole nutmeg to a mortar and break into smaller pieces with a pestle (this is just to make it easier to grind, so don’t worry about being too precise!). Repeat with the cinnamon. Tear the bay leaves into smaller pieces. Transfer all of the spices to a spice grinder and grind into a fine powder (it will be slightly warm when you remove the lid). Transfer to an airtight container (do not cover yet) and let cool completely. Then close the lid.

Do Ahead: Garam masala can be made 1 month ahead. Cover and store in a cool, dark place.

To a small heatproof bowl, add 1 medium yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, 2 Tbsp. lime juice, 2 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 2 tsp. chaat masala, ½ tsp. cayenne powder, and ½ tsp. fine sea salt.

In a small pan over medium-high heat, warm 2 Tbsp. peanut oil or any vegetable oil or avocado oil until it shimmers. Add 1 tsp. cumin seeds and cook until fragrant and they start to turn brown, about 1 minute. Be careful not to let the seeds burn or they will taste bitter. Remove from the heat and pour the hot oil over the onions. Toss to coat the onions in the spice mixture.

Serve immediately or let cool and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.

To a mortar and pestle or food processor, add one 2" (5-cm) piece fresh ginger, chopped, 4 garlic cloves, peeled, and 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, chopped, and pound or pulse into a chunky paste. To a medium bowl, add 2 lb. (910 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs, excess fat trimmed, cut into 2" [5-cm] pieces, along with the ginger-garlic paste and 1 tsp. fine sea salt and toss to combine. Cover and place in the refrigerator to marinate for a minimum of 1 hour or overnight.

In a medium heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-low heat, warm ⅓ cup (80 ml) vegetable oil or avocado oil, then add 1 tsp. cumin seeds, ½ tsp. black mustard seeds, ½ tsp. black peppercorns, 5 whole cloves, 1 fresh or dried bay leaf, 1 star anise, and one 3" [7.5-cm] cinnamon stick, broken into small pieces, and lightly toast and until fragrant, about 1 minute. Increase the heat to medium, add 1 medium red or yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), finely chopped, cover, and cook until the onion is translucent and beginning to turn brown around the edges, stirring halfway through, about 10 minutes.

Add 1 Tbsp. ground coriander, 1 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 1 Tbsp. Garam Masala, 2 tsp. cayenne powder, and 1 tsp. powdered turmeric. Stir to combine and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute. Drain off the excess marinade from the chicken, then add it to the pot along with 3 Tbsp. tomato paste, 1 Tbsp. packed fresh fenugreek leaves, and remaining 1½ tsp. fine sea salt and stir until everything is mixed thoroughly and the chicken is covered with the spices and tomato paste. Add ½ cup (120 ml) water and mix again. Cover and cook until the chicken is cooked through and tender, 30 minutes, stirring halfway through.

Remove from the heat and sprinkle with the remaining 1 tsp. Garam Masala, remaining 1 tsp. fresh fenugreek leaves, and cilantro leaves. Serve immediately with lime wedges, Insanely Addictive Pickled Onions, and steamed rice or Indian flatbread.

Do Ahead: Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days or in the freezer for up to 1 month.

#6494. The Maldon Salt Scandal, Explained

Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly column covering the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the ever-escalating advent calendar wars.

The long-awaited sixth installment of the Grand Theft Auto franchise was released this week. Why in God’s name am I talking about it for a food magazine? Because the game was so highly anticipated that food delivery apps saw noticeable spikes in demand as players stayed home, many skipping work to play the game for hours at a time without breaks for cooking. A Miami cafe even released a specialty roast of coffee beans, and one Florida restaurant chain partnered with Rockstar, the game’s developer, to bring an in-game food spot to life. (The game is set in a fictional state modeled after Florida.)

This is the kind of widespread, obsessively orchestrated marketing plan you’d expect around a Beyoncé album. We have arguably not been this close to a true monocultural moment since The Dress debate in February of 2015.

In other news, Alison Roman’s podcast, Having People Over, which I teased in last week’s Open Tab officially debuted this week. Episode one features Bowen Yang, and the next couple will be with Lauren Graham and Jenny Slate—and then that’s it until 2027, as Roman told me.

Also in today’s Open Tab: the salty, salacious scandal around Maldon’s sourcing, a new study on GLP-1s for children, the case for cocktail brutalism, and a Tuscon restaurant alchemizing desert ingredients.

At Bon Appétit, we love flaky Maldon salt. Like, we really love it. So when a report from The Observer detailed how Maldon’s famed UK sea salt was in fact also made with German rock salt, gasps rippled around the Bon Appétit office. I mean, not gasps exactly, but everyone was like “whaaaat? That’s crazy.”

The gritty details: Maldon’s been harvested in Essex’s Blackwater estuary for more than a century, and the label on each box lists its only ingredient as 100% sea salt. The Observer’s report reveals that the company imports mined rock salt from Germany as part of the “salt-on-salt” process in which the sea salt is enriched with minerals. The company is allowed to call their product 100% sea salt because the salt that comes from mines was at one point in a sea—in prehistoric times.

Origin and processing matters because these factors can affect the final flavor, color, and how salty it tastes. Maldon is a finishing salt, and it's largely prized for the crunch of its big flakes. But consumers don’t love feeling like they’ve been lied to, and judging from the comments under Maldon’s apology post on Instagram, that is precisely how many feel.

I would wager that Maldon will survive this controversy. It’s a legacy brand that’s a staple in professional and home kitchens alike. And while it’s not a great look, I think the majority of consumers would say that salt is salt, and as long as Maldon stays crunchy and salty, they’ll be on board.

Semaglutide, the GLP-1 compound in brand name drugs Wegovy and Ozempic, is already approved for use in children older than 12. But a new study published in the New England Journal of Medicine shows that the drug is effective for treating obesity in kids as young as six. According to the New York Times, drug manufacturer Novo Nordisk, plans to ask the FDA to authorize the drug’s use for kids in that age group.

It's hard to know what the long term effects on developed adult brains and bodies would be, let alone the quickly growing, changing brains and bodies of young kids. We’re beginning to see that GLP-1s can have a profound effect on mental health in adults, but though it seems the drugs can indeed contribute to weight loss in children, there are many other facets of its use that we simply don’t understand and haven’t studied yet.

When I helped build our Best Bars list last year the question of what exactly makes a great bar was one we pondered over for many hours. Order a drink from a Bar of Note (i.e. one of the many bars sitting on a Best-of list somewhere on the internet), and you’ll quickly get a sense of how they answer that same question. Namely: spectacle.

Cocktails across the country and abroad have ramped up in complexity and presentation in recent years fueled mostly by the reason you might expect: spectacle and theatricality performs well on social media, according to a report in the Times.

As a reporter who has often been forced to order the most attention-grabbing, loudest, most obnoxious drink on the menu in the name of journalism—and as a cocktail-enjoyer in my free time—I would like to propose a paradigm shift. Cocktail brutalism. Cocktail minimalism. Cocktail absurdism—actually anything besides the overwhelming maximalist cocktail moment that we’re stepping into. The ideal drink special? A beer, a shot, and a genuine compliment.

At Tuscon’s Ursa, ingredients from the surrounding desert are transformed. Chef Aaron Lopez and June Chee who lead the restaurant see cacti and brittlebrush as deeply flavorful staples of their menu. Read on to see how these ingredients come to life.

#6493. Bakery Tourism Is Booming—These Are The 15 Spots Everyone Wants To Visit

Your next trip might come with a side of cardamom bun.

Bakeries are no longer just a stop along the way—they’re the final destination. According to Yelp’s 2027 Food and Drink Trend report, bakeries are becoming such a hot commodity that people are planning entire trips around viral treats. Yelp searches for “bakeries near me” are up 561% from last year, while searches for a “sweet treat” are up 303%. Treat yo’ self culture is officially here.

Bakery tourism is on the rise, and honestly, I'm not surprised. I, myself, am prone to walking unfamiliar city streets just to get my hands on the town's most beloved pastry. And people are getting pretty specific about what they want. Searches for cardamom buns are up 24%, kouign-amann 67%, and salt bread a whopping 616%.

It’s not just individual pastries getting all the attention, either. Yelp found that searches for “hot and new bakeries” jumped 359%, while “best gluten-free bakery” rose 113%. Bakeries are also the most-saved type of specialty food shop on Yelp’s My Lists feature. Even New York City's Radio Bakery, which you’ll find below, saw searches increase by 176%. It seems we’re all doing some serious research before our next pastry run.

So which hot spots should you add to your must-visit list? I asked Yelp to do a deep dive into the most-saved bakeries across America to see which ones people are bookmarking. Here's what came out on top.

This famed Taiwanese bakery opened its first U.S. outpost earlier this year in Pasadena, California, and has already gone viral for its unique cream cheese-filled bagels and flaky pastries.

What started out as a pandemic-era creation has now morphed into a line-worthy brick-and-mortar. Bad Butter regularly draws block-long lines, with its breads, croissants, and pastries often selling out.

In Santa Ana, California, 61hundred Bread is known for its signature heirloom blue-corn masa sourdough bread, along with Filipino baked goods like pandesal and ube-filled cruffins.

At this New York City French bakery, the jambon-beurre sandwich is the star item. Fresh baguettes and flaky croissants are also among the other reasons locals and tourists flock to the shop.

Located at the Halepuna Waikiki hotel in Honolulu, Hawaii, Halekulani Bakery is known for its signature coconut cake and assortment of pastries.

Located in Los Angeles, California, Out Of Ordi specializes in Korean-style salt bread.

New York City’s Sunday Morning frequently sells out of its viral cinnamon rolls.

San Diego’s Relic Bakery & Kitchen offers a mix of sweet and savory baked goods, from pies and croissants to breads and danishes.

In New York City, you’ll find Justin’s Salt Bread, voted the city’s best new bakery of the year and known for—you guessed it—its salt bread.

San Francisco’s Butter & Crumble is known for its crumble cakes and laminated pastries, with offerings that rotate seasonally.

Another Honolulu bakery makes the list, although this one comes with a twist. Part bakery, part butcher shop, The Local General Store sells everything from quiche and danishes to sausage and ham.

It looks like my travel schedule just got a little busier (and tastier).

Space and time seem like the bedrock of reality. But startling clues are leading physicists toward the possibility that something stranger lies beneath.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Every experience we have and every moment we live unfold naturally across space and time ‪—‬ so naturally that we rarely stop to question their existence.

Physics takes this just as much for granted as we do. For more than 100 years, the field has been built upon the foundational idea that space-time — the four-dimensional fabric of the universe — is fundamental.

But new insights drawn from the hearts of black holes, quantum computers and ultraprecise lasers, are now poised to challenge this assumption, leading a growing number of physicists to ask the same question: What if space and time aren't the bedrock of the universe, but emerge from something even deeper?

"You can build space from a theory without space," Jeff Forshaw, a professor of particle physics at the University of Manchester in the U.K., told Live Science.

For decades, we have known that two extraordinarily successful descriptions of nature are incompatible.

In Einstein's general theory of relativity, matter and energy bend space-time and we experience that curvature as gravity. Quantum mechanics, meanwhile, describes nature on the smallest scales of atoms and subatomic particles.

But quantum mechanics still has no adequate description of the force of gravity. The conflict between these theories of big and small becomes unavoidable in extreme environments, such as the centers of black holes or the smallest fractions of a second after the Big Bang, where gravity grows to be intense on the minute scales ruled by quantum mechanics.

An artist's illustration of the Big Bang with time running from the image's bottom to the top. During the first brief fraction of a second after the Big Bang the universe was so dense that quantum effects and gravity were equally strong.

So far, efforts to combine them mathematically and theoretically have led to nonsensical results.

"They seem not to fit together into a single, consistent framework that we know to be correct," Latham Boyle, a theoretical physicist at the University of Edinburgh in the U.K, told Live Science.

It's possible that one or both of these theories is incomplete, but an increasingly popular belief among physicists is that both theories are perched upon an untested assumption: space-time itself.

Both general relativity and quantum mechanics assume that space-time exists. Yet neither explains why our universe seems to have three dimensions of space and one of time, or where space-time comes from. If this assumption is wrong, the apparent foundation of reality could be a large-scale approximation of something even more mysterious.

In Einstein's model, space-time is a little like how people once viewed water: smooth and continuous, capable of bending and rippling. But water only appears continuous on large scales because we can't see its composite "bits," or individual molecules, said Boyle, whose research explores quantum gravity, the early universe and whether space-time is fundamental or emergent. One proposal is that space-time is similar.

"It seems smooth but only because we can't view it under a fine enough microscope," Boyle told Live Science. Yet no one has found direct evidence for space-time's microscopic "bits." That leaves physicists searching for indirect clues in places where existing theories are pushed to their breaking point: black holes.

At the hearts of black holes, general relativity breaks down by predicting space-time curving infinitely, while quantum physics gives their boundaries baffling properties.

Around black holes gravity (the curvature of space-time) is warped to an infinite degree.

Black holes also offer intriguing clues that space-time, like water, may have microscopic ingredients. One clue comes from thermodynamics ‪—‬ the laws governing heat, temperature and entropy.

Entropy is often described as measuring the disorder in a system, but physicists use it to describe how many hidden microscopic arrangements can produce the same large-scale behavior. A glass of water, for example, may have one temperature and pressure even though its molecules could be moving and arranged in an enormous number of different ways. The more possible microscopic arrangements there are, the greater its entropy.

This matters because thermodynamics usually describes the large-scale behavior of microscopic ingredients. If Einstein’s equations are thermodynamic in nature, their entropy may be due to hidden microscopic states of space-time that physicists cannot yet see.

"General relativity is thermodynamics," Forshaw said. "Einstein's equations are a statement of thermodynamics. They're a statistically emergent feature of an underlying theory."

In the 1970s, Jacob Bekenstein and Stephen Hawking showed that black holes, too, have entropy and a physical temperature. This raised striking questions: Are there microscopic ingredients that account for those thermodynamic properties, and if so, what are they?

If those constituents exist, then space-time's smooth geometry, like the continuous appearance of water, emerges only on larger scales.

Another clue is that Einstein's equations appear to contain traces of this hidden structure, somehow reproducing the relationships needed for black holes to have a temperature, even though the theory directly connects the shape of space-time only to the matter it contains.

"Einstein's equation, which we thought was just a classical equation, nothing to do with quantum mechanics, seems to secretly know — or at some level to have known — about this finite entropy associated with the black hole," Boyle said.

The entropy of black holes also gives rise to a second sign that space-time emerges from something deeper: a puzzle known as the black hole information paradox.

Stephen Hawking in front of a projection of the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy formula for black holes.

Quantum mechanics says that physical information can never be destroyed. Yet if black holes emit radiation — an idea famously proposed by Stephen Hawking in 1974 — they should slowly evaporate. This is a profound contradiction: A black hole's Hawking radiation is thermal, depending solely on its mass, electric charge and angular momentum. It contains no obvious record of what originally fell inside. That means that if the black hole eventually disappears, the information of what it once gobbled up seems to vanish with it.

But a black hole's entropy scales not with the three-dimensional volume enclosed by it but with the two-dimensional area of its event horizon, the point beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape. Therefore, it's possible that all the information within any region might somehow be stored on its boundary. This became known as the holographic principle, named after a hologram, in which a 3D image is encoded on a 2D surface.

In 1997, theoretical physicist Juan Maldacena made the idea mathematically precise. He showed that a higher-dimensional theory containing gravity could be mapped onto a lower-dimensional quantum theory without it.

The two descriptions appeared to be interchangeable, equally valid views of reality. But some researchers now go further: They think the lower-dimensional quantum theory may be the fundamental description, while the higher-dimensional space-time we seem to live in is what emerges when its information is decoded.

These ideas gave rise to holography. Its central principle is that a gravitational world in more dimensions may be completely encoded by a quantum theory without gravity in fewer dimensions. That lower-dimensional theory lives on the boundary of the higher-dimensional spacetime.

You should think of the lower-dimensional thing as being what's most real

Mark Van Raamsdonk, a professor of physics at the University of British Columbia, compares the concept to a computer's memory chip. At the fundamental level, a video game is encoded in physical bits switching between states. Yet on a screen, those bits produce a representation of a 3D world containing objects, movement and physical rules. The virtual world seems spatially real, even though its underlying information is stored very differently.

"You should think of the lower-dimensional thing as being what's most real," Van Raamsdonk told Live Science.

Quantum entanglement may play a central role in how this lower-dimensional information gives rise to higher-dimensional space-time. It describes how particles can share linked quantum properties, even when separated by vast distances.

"If I want to decode what space-time geometry is being stored by the quantum state of this lower-dimensional system, all I need to do is probe this entanglement structure," Van Raamsdonk said.

For decades, directly testing this theory appeared hopeless. Physicists thought they would need particle collisions approaching the Planck scale — the fantastically high energy at which quantum effects are expected to become as important as gravity, and far beyond anything existing colliders can produce.

But physicists realized they don't need to rely on brute force. They are now developing several ways around that energy barrier.

The CMS (Compact Muon Solenoid) detector at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. Reaching the Planck scale requires roughly 900 trillion times more energy than the Large Hadron Collider can produce.

How could scientists discover whether space-time has a deeper structure? One way is to search for a subtle jitter, or static hum, in space-time itself. Experiments such as GQuEST, a collaboration involving Fermilab and Caltech, and QUEST at Cardiff University in the U.K. split laser light along different paths and recombine it. Extraordinarily small changes in the distance light travels may reveal fluctuations, arising from discrete building blocks of space-time, that are consistent with some of holography's models.

In some holographic models, physicists represent the underlying units of information as quantum bits (qubits) — mathematically identical to those used in quantum computers. Physically, a computer qubit may be encoded in an ion or electrical circuit, whereas a qubit in a holographic model represents a possible microscopic unit of the quantum theory from which space-time emerges. This equivalence allows quantum processors to simulate space-time models.

In such models, the patterns of entanglement between the qubits dictate the physical distances between regions of space. The stronger those entanglements are, the closer together two corresponding regions are; if the entanglements are severed, the space-time between them tears apart.

QUEST compares measurements from two neighboring laser beam splitters, or interferometers. Some theoretical models predict quantum fluctuations of space-time that would affect both instruments in a related way. Researchers therefore search for matching fluctuations in their measurements while working to rule out shared sources of laboratory noise. Finding the predicted pattern could support those models; finding nothing would constrain how strong such fluctuations could be, killing off flawed models and refining how microscopic components (or chunks of information) translate into space-time's geometry.

Atom interferometers such as AION and MAGIS-100 extend the search for quantum jitters by using atoms as sensitive probes. When a laser pulse hits an atom, the atom enters superposition, in which it is simultaneously in two different locations at once. It then travels along two separate paths before being recombined by a final pulse. If space-time fluctuates slightly differently along one path than the other, a measurable shift is detected in the atom's interference pattern.

The cold-atom preparation and trapping apparatus for the strontium atom source in Fermilab's Matter-wave Atomic Gradiometer Interferometric Sensor (MAGIS-100).

Another approach called BMV experiments (after the surnames of their independent developers Sougato Bose and his collaborators, Chiara Marletto and Vlatko Vedral) take diamond nanocrystals weighing around a hundred-billonth of a kilogram and place them into a state of quantum superposition.

Painstakingly shielded from every possible electromagnetic and nuclear interaction, and placed at different distances from one another, the diamonds are put through a key test. If they emerge from the experiment with the electron states entangled, then gravity alone produced the entanglement.

That would be evidence that gravity can transmit quantum effects — something a classical gravitational field could not produce. And if gravity (the curvature of space-time) can exist in superposition, it could be a strong clue that space-time's geometry is woven out of quantum information. The challenge, so far, is in excluding all the other effects that may obscure the signal.

On cosmic scales, future gravitational wave observatories ‪—‬ including the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna, the Einstein Telescope and the Cosmic Explorer ‪—‬ could scrutinize gravity at the first clues' source: around black holes. After two black holes merge, the resulting object settles down by emitting gravitational waves with characteristic frequencies and decay times. Einstein's theory makes precise predictions for this "ringdown," allowing researchers to search for discrepancies.

An artist's illustration for how the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) will detect ripples in space-time created by merging black holes.

Such discrepancies could potentially point to the quantum nature of space-time near black holes. Interpreting them would require distinguishing between competing explanations ‪—‬ an unexpected signal could cryptically hint at space-time's underlying nature, but it wouldn't reveal a direct picture of its microscopic ingredients.

To identify the bits that make up the reality beneath space-time, scientists are also turning to quantum computers. By entangling many qubits in specific ways to mimic different models of emergent space-time, scientists could determine which mathematical models of the constituent bits are more likely.

"The study of many-body, highly entangled systems is where the future of this whole enterprise is," Forshaw said.

Precursor tests are already underway. In 2022, for example, Google's Sycamore quantum processor was used to reproduce the behavior of a simple theoretical wormhole — not by creating a real hole in space-time but by arranging nine qubits so that their behavior could also be described using gravity.

Earlier this year, researchers went further, using the trapped-ion quantum computer IonQ Forte to test how something resembling gravitational geometry could emerge from patterns of quantum information. The qubits in Forte were arranged into a model that could be interpreted in two connected ways: both as a network of quantum information and as a simple holographic geometry. The researchers then altered the entanglement between the qubits. In the model’s gravitational interpretation, this was akin to adding mass. Just as adding mass bends Einstein's space-time, the researchers expected changing the entanglement to alter the corresponding geometry — and it did.

The findings demonstrate that researchers can study a mathematical relationship between entanglement and geometry using quantum hardware. However, they do not establish that our space-time emerges from lower-dimensional quantum information.

"The experiment that we did is a baby step in that direction," Crystal Noel, an experimental physicist at Duke University who led the experimental side of the project, told Live Science. One limitation of this result is that it reproduces features of a simplified, static theoretical universe, rather than the expanding universe in which we live. Testing a more realistic model of the universe might require entangling 100 or 200 qubits, which may be possible in the near future.

Each of these experiments will probe different aspects of the relationship between gravity and quantum physics, although none would by itself prove that space-time emerges from information. Taken together, however, their results could begin to reveal what theories of quantum gravity match the real world — and whether emergent space-time is among them.

Such a discovery would raise profound questions not only about the universe’s foundations, but about what it means for anything — including ourselves — to exist within it.

"If I tell you that space doesn't exist, it really questions what it means to be," Forshaw said. "How can you actually talk about things when there's no space to put things in?"

#6490. Cranberry Meringue Pie

A big, billowing cloud of meringue tops this crimson beauty and acts as a sweet reprieve from the tart cranberry curd. The vibrant filling is made even more sour with a generous amount of lime juice. Think lemon meringue pie but holiday-ified. Use our Perfect Pie Crust as the base to create a sturdy-flaky foundation, and be sure to start the pie the day before you plan to serve it, as the curd requires several hours of chilling to set into a sliceable texture. Cut into it too soon and it will run onto your plate, creating a messy—albeit delicious—slice.

We never make pie dough without a metal bench scraper. Our favorite is from Gestura. Use the scraper to cut butter, fold dough and nudge it into shape, transfer it from counter to plastic wrap, trim edges, cut strips, and, sure, scrape flour off your counter.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

3 hours (plus 30 minutes for freezing and 5 hours for chilling)

Whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour and dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more rice flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Let dough disk sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Roll out dough on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1½" overhang. Fold overhang under so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Set pan on a rimmed baking sheet and prick bottom and sides of crust with a fork in several places. Freeze, uncovered, at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 400°. Line crust with a sheet of parchment paper and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake crust, tenting edges with foil if browning too quickly, until edges are set and look dry, 20–25 minutes. Carefully lift out parchment paper and weights and continue baking crust, gently pressing bottom and sides occasionally with a flat-bottomed measuring cup if puffing up, until bottom looks dry and is golden, 20–25 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let crust cool.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Bring 1 lb. fresh or frozen cranberries, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, and ¼ cup water to a boil in a large saucepan, then reduce heat to medium and simmer, stirring often, until cranberries soften and burst and most of the liquid has evaporated, 10–15 minutes. Let cranberry mixture cool.

Transfer cranberry mixture to a blender; reserve pan. Add ⅔ cup fresh lime juice and ¼ cup (32 g) cornstarch and blend on high speed until smooth. Scrape purée back into pan (not over heat) and add 3 large eggs, 2 large egg yolks, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Place over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture bubbles and thickens to a pudding-like consistency, about 4 minutes. Remove pan from heat. Add ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, and whisk until melted and combined. Strain curd through a fine-mesh sieve, pushing with a rubber spatula, directly into crust. Smooth into an even layer and cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Chill pie at least 4 hours and up to 1 day.

Just before serving, beat 6 large egg whites, room temperature, ¼ tsp. cream of tartar, remaining 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until foamy and sugar is dissolved, about 5 minutes. Increase speed to high and continue to beat until stiff peaks form, about 3 minutes more.

Spoon meringue over filling and swirl decoratively as desired. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue if desired.

#6488. Costco's Thanksgiving Dinner Kit Is Officially Back—Here's What It Comes With

The turkey, the sides, and a whole lot less holiday stress.

Depending on who you are, cooking a full Thanksgiving dinner can bring either excitement or complete dread. If you fall into the latter camp, Costco is here to help with its newest offering in the deli department.

Laura Lamb of @costcohotfinds shared on social media that the warehouse’s Thanksgiving dinner kit has officially returned for 2026. The prepared meal includes all the holiday essentials, with much of the prep work already taken care of.

Each kit comes with a seasoned half turkey breast over a bed of herbed stuffing, along with Yukon Gold mashed potatoes, green beans, cranberry sauce, and gravy. Costco is pricing the meal at just $3.99 per pound, which works out to around $40 to feed seven to eight people.

The label includes simple instructions for preparing all the components. The uncooked turkey, naturally, takes the most time. Since it’s placed over the stuffing, the turkey drippings add even more flavor and moisture as it roasts in the oven.

The warehouse keeps this dinner kit pretty consistent from year to year, although one Costco shopper wasn’t as impressed with a particular component this time around. Costco fan and content creator @photogami reports that the gravy is a bit underseasoned and not as good as it was last year. (Thankfully, this issue has a pretty easy solution.)

Lamb also noted that you’ll still need to buy a few extras to round out the meal, like dinner rolls and pumpkin pie. And if you’re a stuffing lover, the amount that comes in Costco’s kit might not be enough for you.

Still, it’s hard to argue with the price and convenience—and members are already eager to pick up a kit for their own holiday celebrations. “Got this last year and it was all absolutely delicious,” one user on Instagram wrote. “Highly recommend.” Another commented, “This is such a great idea for a smaller Thanksgiving!”

If you want to grab a kit for yourself, plan accordingly. All Costco locations are closed on Thanksgiving Day, so you only have a few days to snag one.

#6486. 37 Thanksgiving Cocktails and Drinks for Every Guest

Whether you’re pouring a cup of cheer or drinking to steel your nerves against Great-Aunt Edna, these Thanksgiving cocktails cover every angle. There are the cranberry, apple, and maple flavors we crave this time of year, plus big-batch drinks that won’t keep you playing bartender all afternoon. We’re talking freezer-ready martinis, bourbon punch, and a cranberry mule that guests can spike themselves. After all, your to-do list is long enough.

And since Thanksgiving is something of a marathon, we’ve included lighter aperitifs and nonalcoholic drinks for anyone looking to pace themselves—or skip the booze altogether. When dinner gives way to dessert, warm up with a hot buttered rum, mulled wine, or spiced apple cider. Just don’t forget to set out a few Thanksgiving appetizers while you’re at it.

Save recipes and plan every week with confidence. Download the app

We love a Paper Plane as much as the next discerning cocktail drinker, but shaking them up one at a time? Hard pass. Batch the bourbon, Aperol, and amaro for this Thanksgiving cocktail ahead, then stir in the lemon juice and water about an hour before serving.

The “upside-down” refers to the inverted ratio of gin and vermouth in these martinis (not what they’ll do to you). The result is a lighter-drinking cocktail you can batch ahead and stash in the freezer until guests arrive.

All the steeped, spiced flavors you love in a hot toddy, with none of the warmth. This icy twist keeps pre-dinner cocktail hour refreshingly chill. Relatives, take note.

Apple cider, tart cranberry juice, and spicy ginger ale give rum punch a seasonal makeover. Make the cranberry-studded ice cubes ahead of time; they’ll keep the punch cold and make each glass look party-ready.

Sure, a cold beer works fine while you're watching football or tending the turkey fryer. But a pitcher of crisp Mexican lager punched up with margarita citrus makes the occasion feel a little more festive. For another low-effort beer cocktail, try a Spaghett—just lager, Aperol, and lemon.

For a big-batch cocktail with a distinctly autumnal spin, combine rum with dry hard cider and fruit. Prepare the rum base ahead, but save the bubbly cider until just before serving to preserve its fizz.

Bourbon, cognac, floral Earl Grey tea, and an herb-honey syrup make a party-ready punch. For an eye-catching presentation, add an ice ring decorated with lemon slices and rosemary sprigs.

Mezcal, orange liqueur, honey, and chocolate bitters make a lightly smoky cocktail that's particularly good with dessert. Even better, you can batch eight servings and stash them in the freezer up to two weeks ahead. No last-minute shaking required.

Feeling a little gung-ho about Christmas’s fast approach, are we? A big-batch punch packed with cranberry, citrus, nutty sherry, and warming spices makes a delicious bridge between Thanksgiving and the winter holidays.

A seasonal riff on the French 75 swaps gin for bourbon and adds a homemade pear syrup spiced with cinnamon, ginger, and cloves. We like it for a sparkling toast before dinner or alongside pie afterward.

The season of Hallmark’s flannel-clad himbos calls for a drink to match. Enter this lower-ABV sipper made with apple cider and amaro. A little bitter, a little sweet, and just fizzy enough—rather like the male lead in whatever movie “your aunt” is watching.

Homemade cranberry-thyme syrup gives this sparkling cocktail its ruby-red glow. A little Campari adds a pleasantly bitter edge, while Champagne makes it worthy of a holiday toast. The syrup can be prepared up to two weeks ahead.

If you want to start Thanksgiving with a little bubbly, this three-ingredient, lower-ABV aperitif is a fine place to begin. The recipe serves four, and the ginger syrup can be made well in advance.

Replace the gin in a classic Negroni with sparkling wine and you’ve got a lighter, fizzy aperitif. The bubbles mellow Campari’s bitter edge, making this a friendly introduction for the Negroni-curious.

Two ingredients, one very good drink. Fino sherry and ginger ale make a lightly boozy, pleasantly dry cocktail with just enough ginger bite.

Botanical gin, bittersweet grapefruit, and sparkling sake make a bubbly cocktail that’s bright enough to cut through a rich Thanksgiving spread. It serves six, so you can pour a round without mixing drinks one by one.

We love a margarita riff no matter the season. Ginger and rosemary bring a distinctly autumnal edge to this fizzy version, with just enough sparkle to make it feel like a holiday toast.

No punch bowls, cocktail shakers, or complicated mixology required for this two-ingredient drink. You’ve got better things to do between hosting duties and getting all those Thanksgiving sides to the table.

A lower-ABV sipper is your friend during a long day of polite frivolities. The Adonis sounds hella sexy, and we love the earthy nuttiness of sherry and sweet vermouth, made spritzy with club soda.

On a holiday where cranberries overflow-eth, pour a drink to match. Tart, citrusy, and just sweet enough, this vodka cocktail gets its signature pink hue from cranberry juice. A bright counterpoint to all that rich Thanksgiving food.

A classic old-fashioned needs just bourbon or rye, sugar, and bitters. Making drinks for a crowd? Follow our big-batch old-fashioned method to prep ahead and avoid playing bartender all Thanksgiving.

Think of this as an apple-brandy riff on the Manhattan. Sweet vermouth rounds out the fruit’s warmth, making this a particularly fitting fall cocktail.

Not quite a whiskey sour, not quite a cider cocktail, this autumnal drink mixes apple brandy with lemon and orange juices, maple syrup, and a dusting of nutmeg. It tastes like fall without leaning too heavily on baking spices.

Impress your whiskey-loving dad with a Prohibition-era cocktail he may not have heard of. Juicy grapefruit and floral honey give bourbon a bright, citrusy lift, just as winter citrus season is getting underway.

Bourbon, lemon juice, and simple syrup make a tart, boozy drink that’s just sweet enough. It’s ideal for anyone with a minimally stocked bar and a preference for the classics.

Think of the Boulevardier as the Negroni’s bourbon-loving cousin. Whiskey takes the place of gin, bringing warmth and richness to the bittersweet combination of Campari and sweet vermouth. A fine choice for sipping before dinner.

A smoky mezcal cocktail with Earl Grey tea syrup and grapefruit liqueur, this bright, aromatic margarita riff is an intriguing choice for Thanksgiving brunch—or for guests who prefer tequila to bourbon at cocktail hour.

A homemade cranberry-orange jam gives this tequila cocktail a distinctly Thanksgiving twist. Lime juice keeps it tart, while a sugar-salt-and-five-spice rim adds a fragrant finish. Make the jam ahead to streamline cocktail hour.

Whether for your Thanksgiving pregame or tomorrow morning’s hair of the dog, a well-made Bloody Mary is always welcome. Worcestershire, horseradish, hot sauce, and fresh lemon give this savory classic its signature kick.

A packed to-do list is no match for this make-ahead drink. Simmer red wine, cider, fruit, and spices ahead of time, then add tawny port and gently reheat when your guests arrive. Keep it warm in a slow cooker for self-service away from the kitchen.

We’d welcome a pot of mulled apple cider at any fall gathering. It’s nonalcoholic, serves a crowd, and fills the kitchen with the scent of warming spices. Guests can add a tipple of brandy, bourbon, Calvados, or rum if they wish.

Can’t decide between hot cider and spice-rich chai? Have both. This cozy, nonalcoholic drink brings tea and warming spices to apple cider, making it a particularly good companion for a second slice of pie.

For those who’d rather drink their Thanksgiving dessert, a warm mug of dark rum, butter, sugar, and spices delivers the goods. It’s rich, fragrant, and an excellent reason to linger at the table after the pie plates are cleared.

Blood orange, ginger, cinnamon, and cloves make this sweet-tart, nonalcoholic drink feel right at home on Thanksgiving. Prepare the shrub ahead, then top with sparkling water when guests arrive.

Who says a nonalcoholic spritz can’t have a little attitude? A bittersweet alcohol-free aperitif and a splash of olive brine give this savory, citrusy drink plenty of complexity. Serve it very cold, with an olive garnish.

Green tea, lemon juice, fresh mint, and honey make a soothing tonic after the Thanksgiving bacchanal. Alcohol-free on its own, it can take a splash of mezcal if anyone wants to steer it into cocktail territory.

Spiced maple syrup and cranberry juice reimagine the typical Moscow mule as a Thanksgiving drink that skips the vodka. Note that Angostura bitters contain alcohol; for a completely alcohol-free version, use an alternative like All the Bitter.

#6484. Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie

The one thing that can make classic apple pie better? Caramel! That it’s laced with a generous dose of bourbon vaults it straight into hall-of-fame territory. Made using a double batch of our never-fail Perfect Pie Crust, this pretty lattice-topped pie is a crowd-pleaser, familiar enough to appeal to the traditionalists with just enough of a surprise from the booze and the smoky burnt sugar to make the thrill-seekers come back for more. Like all good things, apple pie can’t be rushed. It needs time to chill, bake, and rest—so plan ahead, especially if it’s for Thanksgiving.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling)

Whisk 3⅓ cups (417 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 4 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ½ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour; dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Divide dough in half and pat each piece into a ½"-thick disk. Wrap each disk tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap each disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and ½ cup water in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot and cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat (no need to stir); cook until sugar is dissolved, 4–7 minutes total. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring or swirling pot occasionally, until caramel turns a deep golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Add zest of 1 lemon, 3 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 6 large), peeled, cored, quartered, thinly sliced crosswise, ½ cup bourbon, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes.

Stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes.

Meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes.

Unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers.

Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

Can you name all 12 dinosaurs in this science quiz?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Before an asteroid slammed into Earth 66 million years ago, dinosaurs had roamed our planet for more than 160 million years.

They emerged around 230 million to 240 million years ago, during the Triassic period, when the supercontinent Pangaea had united the landmasses. As Pangaea broke apart, dinosaurs went on to inhabit continents all over the world, including what became Antarctica, which was a temperate rainforest during the Cretaceous period.

Dinosaurs lived in diverse ecosystems, from the snowy Arctic to the hot equatorial regions of Gondwana, a supercontinent in the Southern Hemisphere. As dinosaurs evolved in their different environments, they developed distinct defenses and adaptations to help them survive.

Researchers have discovered hundreds upon hundreds of dinosaur species, from the small "dwarf dinosaur" that lived on an island in Transylvania to the hulking, long-necked Dreadnoughtus in Argentina. Can you tell your dinosaurs apart? Take our quiz to find out.

#6479. A Beautiful Cabbage Galette

Cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side. It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried).

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

When dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside.

Melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine.

Unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet.

Spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.)

Bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.

#6477. Brigadeiro (Brazilian Chocolate Truffles)

Brigadeiros are like a cross between fudge and Tootsie Rolls in truffle form. They're easy to make at home, and even easier to pop in your mouth.

As a major chocolate lover, I’ll eat truffles in almost any form. Brigadeiros have the familiar flavor and fudgy center of a really good chocolate truffle, but they’re even easier to make because they don’t require melting any chocolate. Everything happens in one small saucepan, and the only difficult part is waiting for the mixture to chill.

Brigadeiros start with a can of sweetened condensed milk, plus cocoa powder and butter. The butter is key to carrying the flavor of the cocoa powder and giving the bite-sized treats their signature soft bite. They end up as glossy little chocolate balls covered in sprinkles that taste halfway between a chocolate truffle and a piece of fudge: dense and chewy with a deep cocoa flavor and a center so creamy it nearly melts on contact.

Brigadeiros are Brazilian confections made by cooking a mixture of sweetened condensed milk, cocoa and butter until it’s thick. Once cooled, the mixture is rolled into bite-size balls. A Brazilian birthday party isn’t complete without a tray of brigadeiros, but they also show up at weddings, baby showers and holiday gatherings. Some cooks skip the rolling altogether and eat the soft mixture with a spoon, a style called brigadeiro de colher.

In a small saucepan, combine the sweetened condensed milk, cocoa powder and butter. Cook, stirring constantly, on medium-low heat until the mixture is thickened, 8 to 10 minutes. Transfer the mixture to a medium bowl. Refrigerate it, covered, for two hours or until it’s firm enough to be rolled.

Shape the chilled mixture into 1-inch balls. Roll the balls in chocolate sprinkles.

Editor’s Tip: Rub a little butter on your palms before rolling, and grease them again every few balls. This will keep the mixture from sticking and give each truffle a smooth surface.

Keep brigadeiros in an airtight container in the refrigerator. Store them in paper candy cups or in a single layer separated by parchment so they don’t stick together. Cold brigadeiros get firm, so let them sit out for about 15 minutes before serving to bring back their soft, fudgy centers.

Brigadeiros last up to one week in an airtight container in the refrigerator. They taste best within the first few days while the sprinkles are still crisp.

Yes, you can make brigadeiros ahead of time. Cook the chocolate mixture up to two days in advance and keep it covered in the refrigerator, then roll and coat the truffles the day you plan to serve them. If the mixture is too stiff to scoop, let it stand at room temperature for 10 to 15 minutes.

Yes, brigadeiros freeze well. Arrange the rolled truffles on a parchment-lined baking sheet and freeze them until they’re firm, about one hour, then transfer them to an airtight container and freeze them for up to three months. Thaw them overnight in the refrigerator.

When the brigadeiro mixture stays soft and sticky even after chilling, it almost always means that it needs more time on the stove. Scrape it back into the saucepan and cook it over medium-low heat, stirring constantly, for a few more minutes until it thickens and pulls away from the bottom of the pan in one mass. Watch the mixture closely because overcooking will turn it stiff and grainy.

No, brigadeiros won’t work with regular milk. Brigadeiros depend on the concentrated sugar and milk solids in sweetened condensed milk to cook down into a thick fudge that can be rolled. If you’re out of it, you can make your own sweetened condensed milk by simmering whole milk and sugar until the mixture reduces by about half.
